Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

args.description: Optional arguments for the skill

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__delegate_task
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Delegate one task to a T3-owned child agent/subagent of THIS thread and run it with only the supplied task prompt, without copying parent conversation history. Choose providers and models from orchestrator_capabilities, which uses the same live catalog as the composer. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use this for any model missing from the native tool, including same-provider work, for cross-provider work, or for explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call delegate_task again with the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in the task prompt. Track each round by its own taskId and use a distinct clientRequestId per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use t3_thread_send on its childThreadId. Set isolation to worktree for a separate checkout based on the parent local commit, with project setup completed before the child starts. Uncommitted edits are not copied; omitted isolation shares the parent checkout. Use delegate_task when model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty inheritedOptions from orchestrator_capabilities, even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Set target.options using advertised IDs: Claude {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Check providerInstanceId, model, and options in the result. Provider/model and modes inherit unless overridden. Options inherit only for the same instance and model; explicit entries override individual values and [] or {} clears them. A requested runtimeMode must be one the target provider lists in orchestrator_capabilities runtimeModes; an inherited one steps down to the broadest mode it offers. Leave runtimeMode unset unless the user asks for a supervised child: approval-required and auto-accept-edits usually make the child wait for a person at each action that needs approval. Prefer mode='async' for long work; mode='wait' blocks until completion, a blocking question, a pending approval, or timeout. If hasPendingQuestion, pass threadId=childThreadId to t3_pending_request_list, t3_pending_request_read (with requestId) and t3_pending_request_respond, or ask the user; the task's completion still wakes this thread. If pendingApproval is set, read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback. It grants no approval authority; decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder, and pending request tools answer questions only. The child keeps running and its completion still wakes this thread. timeoutMs on mode=wait is only the parent's wait budget and does not cancel the child. waitTimedOut on that wait call means the timeout fired; keep that taskId and read status on later task_status. An async child's completion wakes this thread through a notification, steered into active turns where supported or queued otherwise, so end the turn instead of polling or spawning watchers; use task_status only when the result is needed mid-turn.

anyOf.description: Model options from orchestrator_capabilities. For the same provider instance and model, overrides individual inherited values; [] or {} clears them. Claude: {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex: {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Only use options advertised by the selected model.
Defaults to shared: use the parent's checkout. Worktree creates a separate checkout from the parent's current local commit before starting the child. Uncommitted edits are not copied.

Defaults to async. Use wait only when this turn needs the child's result before you can continue. A blocking question or a pending approval in the child ends the wait early with the task still running.

timeoutMs.description: Wait budget for mode=wait only. Default 10 minutes. Elapsing it returns waitTimedOut=true on that call and does not cancel the child.

anyOf.description: Defaults to inherit; omit it unless the user asks for a supervised child. A narrower mode is not a read-only switch: on most providers, approval-required and auto-accept-edits pause the child at each action that needs approval until a person approves it in the child's thread, which this thread cannot do. To limit what the child does, say so in the task. A mode ranked above this thread's is rejected; that ranking does not promise the child's provider permissions are narrower than this thread's.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_preview
tools.description: Render an HTML page in T3's headless browser and get back a PNG screenshot, contentHeight (the height the page needs at this width), and its console output: log, info, warning, error, and uncaught exceptions, with stack traces pointing into page.html. console.log is a fine way to report your own checks. Use it to check and iterate on a page before html_render. The first preview on a machine can report that T3 is still installing its preview browser; call again a minute later. Write one self-contained document with inline <style> and <script>. Local images written as absolute file paths (src="/abs/shot.png", CSS url(/abs/bg.webp), or a JS string) are inlined automatically; remote http(s) URLs, such as a CDN chart library, load as-is. The page gets the theme variables and layout described in html_render.

anyOf.description: Viewport width in CSS pixels, 240-1600. Defaults to 728, the reply column; use about 390 to check phones.
Theme to preview. Defaults to dark.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_render
tools.description: Show a finished HTML page (chart, table, diagram, collage, mockup) inline in this thread, above your final text reply; call it before writing that reply. The reader already sees the page, so the reply should not announce it, say where it is, or restate it: add only what the page doesn't say. Preview with html_preview first. T3 fits the frame to the page's height at each reader's width. On mobile, a height below the page's contentHeight caps the frame there, and the rest scrolls inside it; web and desktop fit the whole page, up to 20000px. Write one self-contained document with inline <style> and <script>. Local images written as absolute file paths (src="/abs/shot.png", CSS url(/abs/bg.webp), or a JS string) are inlined automatically; remote http(s) URLs, such as a CDN chart library, load as-is. The frame is borderless on the thread's background, as wide as the reply column (728px on desktop by default, wider if the reader widens chat, about 360px on phones), and its left edge lines up with your reply text. The page sits on the thread's own background, so by default leave html, body, and the outermost element with no background color. This overrides general style preferences such as a fixed black page background. Use a fluid width with no horizontal padding on the outermost element, and no outer card, border, or banner title: the page is part of your reply. If a box needs its own background (a mock of a specific screen, a panel that must stand apart), give it at least 16px of padding on every side and var(--radius) corners, so content never touches its edge. Give charts fixed pixel heights rather than heights that scale with width. Let content set the page's height. The frame grows to fit the page, so a height that follows the viewport makes it grow again and again: html_preview and html_render reject vh, svh, lvh, and dvh units, and height:100% on html or body has the same problem. T3 injects its active theme as CSS custom properties on :root, and they follow the user's theme and light/dark mode live: --background (page background, identical to the thread around the frame), --foreground, --muted, --muted-foreground, --card, --card-foreground, --popover, --popover-foreground, --secondary, --secondary-foreground, --border, --input, --ring, --primary, --primary-foreground (solid buttons), --accent, --accent-foreground (brand accent), --accent-surface, --accent-surface-foreground, --destructive, --destructive-foreground, --destructive-surface, --warning, --warning-foreground, --warning-surface, --success, --success-foreground, --info, --info-foreground, --code-background, --code-foreground, --chart-1 ... --chart-6 (categorical series for charts), --radius, --font-sans, --font-mono. The base stylesheet sets html background/color/font from these, body margin to 0, and hides the page's scrollbar; your own CSS overrides it.

title.description: Short name for the page.

height.description: The frame height in CSS pixels, 80-2000. Use html_preview's contentHeight. A lower height makes long content scroll inside the frame on mobile only.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__orchestrator_capabilities
tools.description: List the V2 provider instances, a short list of their models from the same live catalog as the composer, inherited runtime settings, and app-owned orchestration features available to this caller. The list has the user's favorite and custom models, your own model, every current Codex, Claude, Muse and Grok model, and the first 8 current models of other providers. Other legacy models are left out. omittedModels counts models left out; pass search, such as 'sonnet 4.6', to find them. delegate_task accepts any catalog model, listed or not. For a separate top-level thread in a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_background_wait
tools.description: Keep this thread in the user's Working list and out of their inbox while you wait for background work. Start a background command or Monitor first. Call this before you end your turn if you will act on its result when it wakes you. In taskIds, give the ID shown when the task started. The thread stays in Working until the task ends. The user is not told the work is done. Do not mark work you leave running, such as a dev server or watcher. Unmarked commands and monitors never keep the thread in Working. Pass waiting=false to remove the mark. This does not stop the task. IDs that are not running return in unmatched and change nothing. Only Claude threads support this tool. Other providers return an error.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_worktree_handoff
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Move this agent thread into a new git worktree. To launch a separate agent already bound to a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy instead. Creates the worktree branch (optionally from the base branch's remote), re-points the thread at the worktree, and by default runs the project's setup script there. Changing the workspace detaches the live provider session, so the current turn ends shortly after the handoff is recorded; call this as the last action of the turn. To keep working after the handoff, pass continuationPrompt with the remaining work: it is queued as the thread's next message and starts a new turn inside the worktree with the conversation preserved. Without it the thread stays idle until the next message. The worktree is not removed automatically when the thread is deleted. Fails if the thread is already attached to a worktree.

anyOf.description: Fetch the remote baseRef belongs to and start the worktree branch from its remote-tracking commit instead of the local ref. Defaults to the server's 'new worktrees start from remote' setting.
Run the project's configured setup script in the new worktree after handoff. Defaults to true.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_worktree_list
tools.description: List branch refs and their associated checkout paths for a thread's workspace (omit threadId for this thread) using the app's ref inventory. Detached worktrees without a branch are not included. Use t3_worktree_status for the thread binding and t3_worktree_handoff to create a new worktree.

input.description: Research editor UI juice and motion
input.prompt:
Research task (web), no code changes. I'm designing an interaction-motion identity for Twyne, a literary writing app (local-first rich-text editor + an AI "room of editors" that leave margin notes, a rubric that "stamps" a draft, a stats "Desk" page). Brand: editorial letterpress — paper, ink, type, stamps, vermilion and cobalt, a writers' room. I want motion, shaders and component variants that (a) communicate what an interaction does and whether you should/shouldn't do it (consequence: local vs synced vs sent to an AI provider vs published vs destructive), (b) make the app feel alive, (c) never harm writing performance or legibility, (d) are distinctive versus generic editors (Notion, Google Docs, Word).

Please find and summarise, with source URLs:
1. "Game feel"/"juice" principles applied to productivity UI (e.g. Jonasson & Purho "Juice it or lose it", Rauno Freiberg "Invisible details of interaction design", Emil Kowalski on animation craft, Linear/Raycast/Arc/Things motion writing, Apple HIG motion). Extract concrete, reusable rules (durations, easing, when not to animate, frequency of interaction vs animation budget).
2. Editors with distinctive typing/caret/scroll feel: Microsoft Word smooth caret/typing animation, VS Code smooth caret, iA Writer focus/typewriter mode, Ulysses, Bear, Craft, Obsidian, Monkeytype caret, Typora, Hemingway, Paper by WeTransfer/FiftyThree, Teenage Engineering-style UIs. What exactly do they animate and how is it received (any complaints about distraction/latency)?
3. Ink, paper and letterpress effects on the web: ink-bleed / wet-ink shaders, paper grain/fibre normal maps lit by a moving light, letterpress debossing via CSS, risograph/halftone shaders, stamp impressions. Prefer techniques that are cheap (WebGL fragment shaders at reduced resolution, CSS only, SVG filters) and note performance pitfalls (SVG filters on large areas, backdrop-filter).
4. Modern browser APIs useful here, with current support status (2025-2026): CSS Custom Highlight API (`::highlight()` — which properties are allowed, can it animate?), View Transitions API (same-document), scroll-driven animations (`animation-timeline: scroll()/view()`), `@property` registered custom properties for animating gradients, `linear()` easing for springs, Popover API + `@starting-style`, `interpolate-size`, WebGPU vs WebGL2 availability.
5. Patterns that communicate consequence/trust in UI motion: hold-to-confirm for destructive actions, "sending" vs "saving" animations, rate-limit/out-of-credits states, disabled-with-reason affordances, AI "thinking" indicators that aren't generic spinners (e.g. shimmer text, reading-progress indicators). Note which are considered good vs gimmicky.
6. Anything about "ambient life" in UI: presence indicators (Figma cursors), breathing idle states, time-of-day lighting, and accessibility guidance (prefers-reduced-motion, vestibular triggers, WCAG 2.3.3, avoiding parallax for long reading).

Deliver a compact report (under ~1500 words): bullet points grouped by the six headings, each bullet with a concrete takeaway and a URL. Flag anything you could not verify. Finish with a list of 10 "gaps": ideas that fit a literary editor + AI editors and are rarely done well elsewhere.

input.description: Research editor UI juice and motion
input.prompt:
Research task (web), no code changes. I'm designing an interaction-motion identity for Twyne, a literary writing app (local-first rich-text editor + an AI "room of editors" that leave margin notes, a rubric that "stamps" a draft, a stats "Desk" page). Brand: editorial letterpress — paper, ink, type, stamps, vermilion and cobalt, a writers' room. I want motion, shaders and component variants that (a) communicate what an interaction does and whether you should/shouldn't do it (consequence: local vs synced vs sent to an AI provider vs published vs destructive), (b) make the app feel alive, (c) never harm writing performance or legibility, (d) are distinctive versus generic editors (Notion, Google Docs, Word).

Please find and summarise, with source URLs:
1. "Game feel"/"juice" principles applied to productivity UI (e.g. Jonasson & Purho "Juice it or lose it", Rauno Freiberg "Invisible details of interaction design", Emil Kowalski on animation craft, Linear/Raycast/Arc/Things motion writing, Apple HIG motion). Extract concrete, reusable rules (durations, easing, when not to animate, frequency of interaction vs animation budget).
2. Editors with distinctive typing/caret/scroll feel: Microsoft Word smooth caret/typing animation, VS Code smooth caret, iA Writer focus/typewriter mode, Ulysses, Bear, Craft, Obsidian, Monkeytype caret, Typora, Hemingway, Paper by WeTransfer/FiftyThree, Teenage Engineering-style UIs. What exactly do they animate and how is it received (any complaints about distraction/latency)?
3. Ink, paper and letterpress effects on the web: ink-bleed / wet-ink shaders, paper grain/fibre normal maps lit by a moving light, letterpress debossing via CSS, risograph/halftone shaders, stamp impressions. Prefer techniques that are cheap (WebGL fragment shaders at reduced resolution, CSS only, SVG filters) and note performance pitfalls (SVG filters on large areas, backdrop-filter).
4. Modern browser APIs useful here, with current support status (2025-2026): CSS Custom Highlight API (`::highlight()` — which properties are allowed, can it animate?), View Transitions API (same-document), scroll-driven animations (`animation-timeline: scroll()/view()`), `@property` registered custom properties for animating gradients, `linear()` easing for springs, Popover API + `@starting-style`, `interpolate-size`, WebGPU vs WebGL2 availability.
5. Patterns that communicate consequence/trust in UI motion: hold-to-confirm for destructive actions, "sending" vs "saving" animations, rate-limit/out-of-credits states, disabled-with-reason affordances, AI "thinking" indicators that aren't generic spinners (e.g. shimmer text, reading-progress indicators). Note which are considered good vs gimmicky.
6. Anything about "ambient life" in UI: presence indicators (Figma cursors), breathing idle states, time-of-day lighting, and accessibility guidance (prefers-reduced-motion, vestibular triggers, WCAG 2.3.3, avoiding parallax for long reading).

Deliver a compact report (under ~1500 words): bullet points grouped by the six headings, each bullet with a concrete takeaway and a URL. Flag anything you could not verify. Finish with a list of 10 "gaps": ideas that fit a literary editor + AI editors and are rarely done well elsewhere.

Zen mode turns out to be on by default, which means my screenshot was showing the non-zen view only because I had seeded `zenMode: false`. The real starting experience is the zen one, which strips backgrounds and underlines from persona notes and dims the toolbar. I also see that flow modes exist, with states running from away through working, settling, and flow to stuck, and I'm checking how those get published.

Flow states are published as `html[data-flow]`, so the quiet behavior can be keyed to them: the lamp brightens or dims with each state, stillness in flow, and cards slipping in when stuck. The existing vocabulary should carry that, with the pneumatic post standing for messages going out to the provider and coming back, rather than inventing new metaphors.

The text-surface inventory shows the gaps: no themed selection, no entrance motion on popovers, slash menu or drag overlay, and an off-brand purple drop indicator. I'm reading the existing design docs next so the new grammar builds on the flow states and typewriter-ribbon vocabulary already in the app.

48:## Motion contract
57:Every transition is finite, uses opacity and transform, and returns to fully visible, untransformed content. Nothing waits for animation to become clickable. The component adds no timers, document scans, event listeners, or continuous loading animation. A host should set state for a real action and use `rest` for restored results; key a genuinely new result if the same arrival state must replay.
59:Pass `quiet` during typing and when the instrument is outside the viewport. CSS also respects existing `data-flow="flow"`, `data-flow="settling"`, `data-zen="true"`, and `.zen-mode` ancestors. `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` disables animations and transitions while preserving the same content. No particles, floating idle art, pulse loops, or artificial wait times are used.
61:## Review and reproduction
63:Storybook contains **Instruments / Illustration family** with six size/theme/texture specimens and **Instruments / Meaningful motion** with seven interaction/quiet/theme specimens. Run:
69:Open `/?path=/story/instruments-illustration-family--collection` or `/?path=/story/instruments-meaningful-motion--interactive`. Replay opening, comparison, and result arrival, then enable the quiet checkbox. The example wording and result are a labeled component specimen, not a generated recommendation.
74:- [Short component recording](../public/assets/instruments/motion-study-v1.mp4), suitable as source material for a component demo. It shows a specimen, not a live model or manuscript workflow.
77:The local browser loaded all four alpha assets, with no horizontal overflow at 390px or 1200px. Result and proof-rule animations ended at 240ms and 260ms. Quiet mode produced `animation-name: none` with result opacity 1. The initial reduced-motion check activated the authored media block through CSSOM. A later isolated Playwright pass emulated the browser's `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` preference and exercised Open, Compare and Receive a result: all had zero active animations, `animation-name: none`, and fully visible content. No operating-system settings were changed. These are behavior and visual checks, not a frame-rate benchmark.
87:## Integration boundary
91:## Scene bench implementation
103:Writer-proposed details save in IndexedDB for the exact passage snapshot. They survive reload and stay separate from source evidence. Removal can be undone. Image, sound, and motion buttons **prepare a text brief locally**. The brief contains the exact excerpt and separately labels proposed additions. It does not generate media or send a provider request, and the UI says media generation is not connected to this instrument. Preparing the brief incurs no generation charge; a later external generator can have its own price and data destination.

**Consequence codes:** L = local only (IndexedDB/localStorage). S = syncs to Convex (`markDirty`). AI = sends text to a model provider. P = publishes or shares. D = destructive. V = view only.

## Shared primitives (global.css)
- **`.btn-press`** g:2069-2099: ink fill, typewriter caps, radius 2px, 0.12s transform. Hover turns vermilion-2 with a glow shadow. Active is `translateY(1px) scale(.98)`. Disabled is opacity .4. Focus at g:2156.

- **`.icon-btn`** has two definitions:
  - g:2164-2188: 1.75rem hit target, hover background paper-2, active `scale(.9)`, focus offset 1px.
  - g:4496-4503: redefines the transition (transform + color only, so the background transition is lost) and sets active to `scale(.92)`. The second one wins.
- **`.dept-label`** has two definitions:
  - g:582: typewriter, 0.625rem, letter-spacing .32em, ink-muted.
  - g:4488-4493: adds a letter-spacing transition, and hover sets .22em. So every kicker *tightens* on hover, which is odd for non-interactive labels.
- **`.tool-btn`** g:2191-2217: hover vermilion, active `scale(.95)`. Pressed state (`[aria-pressed=true]`) gets an inset vermilion underline.
- **Other primitives:**
  - `.focus-ring` g:1768: 2px vermilion outline, offset 2px.

  - `ink-bleed` g:4268, `dossier-action-pulse` g:2144, `filed-dossier-arrive` g:687.

## The Drawer (left sidebar)

2. Elements and interactions:

Active row: paper-3 border on paper-soft. Inactive: transparent border with hover paper-soft. Radius 2px, serif. **No transition on active-row change, and no focus-ring style beyond `.focus-ring`.** Consequence L (saves active id); it restarts AI background processes.

The wordmark has an endless four-second wobble, which might be distracting, so I'm considering whether to keep it or stop it while the user is in flow. I also see that the Unpublish and Unpublish from PDS actions currently run without any confirmation step.

I'm noting that the Unpublish, Unpublish from PDS, remove-collaborator, and Discard source actions are destructive and could suit a hold-to-confirm pattern. I also want the two Share entry points to look different, since publishing is public and sharing is with collaborators. The AI actions also need a visual marker showing that they send the passage to an outside provider.

Next I'm working out the motion tokens for the stylesheet, where the durations run from a quick 90ms tick up to a rare 900ms ceremony, plus the house easing curves for ordinary and stamp-style motion.

I'm sketching how each action shows its consequence: local actions stay quiet, sync actions hint at a carbon copy on hover that converges on press, and AI actions get a postmark and a travelling wire effect to signal the passage leaves the device.

I'm defining the hold-to-confirm and consequence treatments: destructive actions get a press-and-hold fill, and publish gets a stamp-style press with a seal outline. Holding a button fills it with ink from left to right over about 700ms, and releasing early drains it, with the keyboard using the same timing.

I'm weighing whether hold-to-confirm is the right pattern here, since it's common in games and mobile apps but timed holds could be hard for some users with motor impairments. I'll check that against the accessibility guidance before committing to it.

I'm settling on a two-step confirm for the destructive actions: the first click arms the button and floods it halfway with ink while the label changes to a confirm prompt, and a second click within a few seconds fires it. Holding the button down also works, filling the ink over about 700ms and firing on completion, so both fast and deliberate users have a path.

I'm working out the desk lamp: a fixed, pointer-transparent light pool that follows the cursor across the workspace, moved with a transform so it stays on the compositor rather than repainting. I'm also weighing whether it should stay off the manuscript page itself or apply everywhere with a subtler gradient.

I'm thinking about the desk lamp's shading next: a vignette overlay that darkens the edges slightly and stays clear in the centre, so the pointer's pool of light reads as brighter without washing out the cream paper. Since the edge darkening is only a few percent, I'll check that it doesn't cost any text contrast on the manuscript.

I'm picturing the page canvas as a fixed background layer beneath a transparent scroller, so the paper texture sits behind the manuscript. For the paper itself, I'm thinking of a procedural fibre shader with elongated noise, lit by the lamp through a bump-like height field, rendered at half resolution and redrawn only when the pointer moves.

I'm weighing whether the lamp shader is worth it over plain CSS, given the user wants a lit paper desk, though the light has to stay subtle enough not to hurt legibility. Outside the page the desk is visible, but in zen mode the page widens and leaves less of it showing, so I'll have to account for that.

I'm planning the lamp's behaviour: the light eases toward the pointer with a damped lag, so it feels like a physical lamp, and it only keeps rendering while it's still moving. I'm also considering whether the light should shift with the time of day, warmer and stronger in the evening and cooler in the morning.

I'm turning to the input channels next, starting with keyboard input as "wet ink": freshly typed text would render slightly blue-black with a faint bleed, then dry over roughly 700ms. I'm thinking about doing this with the CSS Custom Highlight API so the editor's DOM stays untouched, skipping it during IME composition and honouring reduced motion.

I'm weighing a vermilion caret as the editor's red pencil against the ink text, since it's cheap and distinctive, and checking whether vermilion reads clearly on the cream paper. The caret is only a thin line, so it should stay legible without competing with the wet-ink effect.

I'm settling on aubergine for the writer's caret, since that's already the color for the writer's own notes and comments, so "you" stays one consistent hue across the manuscript. I'm weighing whether to keep vermilion as the house accent for the masthead instead.

I'm settling the colour semantics: ink for the manuscript itself, aubergine pencil for the writer's own hand, vermilion for the house, and cobalt for the AI instruments, which already use it for in-flow ticks and the quick review marker.

I'm settling on the wet-ink colour: iron-gall ink goes on blue-black and oxidises to brown-black as it dries, so I'm mixing the ink with a little cobalt for the wet state and letting it settle back to the near-black brown.

content.content:
name: skip-long-verification
description: "Don't block on the full test suite or repeated typecheck runs in twyne; targeted checks only, then hand back"
metadata:
  type: feedback

In twyne, don't run the full `bun run test` suite (it takes over 10 minutes) or keep re-running `tsc` after every edit. When the work is done, stop and report back.

**Why:** On 2026-10-11 the user stopped a persona/voice redesign while it waited on the full suite and said "stop with the typechecking, move on without the tests."

**How to apply:** Run only the targeted test files for the code you changed, at most once, and only if they're quick. Never wait in a loop for long suites. In the summary, say which checks you skipped.
name: autonomy-by-default
description: "Twyne should act on its own by default — reviews, research, editor readings run without the writer clicking; buttons are optional overrides"
metadata:
  type: feedback

Twyne's default is autonomous, fluid action: editors read, research runs, reviews complete, and results arrive without the writer having to press a button. Manual controls may exist as options (re-run, steer, decline), but a feature that waits for a click before doing its core job is a design defect.

**Why:** The user (Keith Noel's product direction, restated by the owner 2026-10-20) said "waiting for the user to click a button is not what I want for this app… the default is autonomous fluid action."

**How to apply:** When building or fixing a feature, ask "does this happen if the writer never clicks?" If not, add an automatic trigger (on draft change / idle / panel open / folio open) with spend guards (dedupe per draft fingerprint, rate floors, session caps) rather than a call-to-action button. Empty states should say what the app is about to do on its own, not invite a click. Hosted (non-BYOK) users must get the autonomous path too. Related: [[skip-long-verification]].
name: no-reflexive-hedging
description: "Don't attach trust/uncertainty caveats to every claim in designs or product copy (e.g. \"sources aren't trustworthy\" on research cards)"
metadata:
  type: feedback

Don't hedge every claim. When proposing features (research cards, extraction, judgements), state what they do; skip stock caveats like "this doesn't make the source trustworthy" or "say so on the card".

**Why:** User pushed back on exactly that line in a Clairic/research-cards proposal (2026-10-20): "we don't need to hedge every claim here."

**How to apply:** Mention a limitation only when it changes the design or a decision. Related: [[autonomy-by-default]].
name: dev-machine-is-old
description: "The user's dev laptop (Intel Iris Xe, Alder Lake) is old; slow local-model results on it are not a reason to drop a feature"
metadata:
  type: feedback

The user's dev laptop has an Intel Alder Lake CPU with Iris Xe integrated graphics, and the user considers it old. When LFM3-Audio ran at 0.32× real time on it (2026-10-29), the user said: "it might be too slow on cpu that is kind of fine this is a pretty old computer so newer machines should be much faster."

**Why:** the target users have newer hardware: dedicated GPUs and Apple silicon.

**How to apply:**
- Don't gate local AI or audio features on real-time performance on this machine.
- Build the feature, and choose the fastest correct path per device with an on-device benchmark, following [[autonomy-by-default]].
- When something can't keep up, show an honest slow-device state.
- Correctness still has to be verified here; only speed is waived.

I also want to check similar work online for gaps, and keep going until every component has some way to give the user a bit of joy.

I'm treating this as both a design and implementation job: a reusable system of motion and feedback, plus a per-component plan for giving each surface some joy, with before-and-after comparisons to show the result. The editor needs its own identity, reacting to how I move, type, scroll, and drag. I also want the app to feel alive, and I'll document the choices I make along the way.

I'm weighing whether to delegate implementation to parallel worktree lanes, since those start from the last commit and won't see my uncommitted edits. The working tree already holds someone else's changes, so I'll leave those alone and keep my work separate.

I'm weighing whether to split the work into parallel worktree lanes, but the core motion system and shared CSS are interdependent and would likely collide if several agents edited them at once. I'll build the foundation myself in a dedicated stylesheet first, then consider handing off file-disjoint component lanes once the tokens exist.

I'm sketching out the motion identity now, starting from Twyne's print-shop feel: wet ink that dries, and type being set, which I'll translate into the timing and easing of the interface.

I'm sketching the motion vocabulary from the print shop itself: ink that wets and dries, type being set and locking up, a press impression when a key is pressed, paper that slides and gets filed or pinned, and messages that arrive through the pneumatic tube. The typewriter ribbon that FlowRibbon already uses is another thread to build on, and I'm working out how the desk ledger should feel as a page.

I'm listing more of the physical vocabulary now: numbers that tick over like a mechanical counter, a wax seal pressed for publishing, and the blue and red pencil marks editors use. I'm also thinking about a rubber stamp for filed or approved items and a desk lamp whose light shifts warmer toward evening. The last idea is blotting paper: when a save happens, the wet ink of recent edits dries, so unsaved text reads as wet and saved text as dry.

I'm thinking about whether the wet-ink idea would be too distracting, and I'm leaning toward a subtle version where newly typed characters look slightly deeper and glossier, then settle into normal ink over about a second. Building that in ProseMirror would mean tracking recently inserted ranges and adding decorations for them, and I'm weighing whether that per-keystroke cost is acceptable if I keep the tracked set small.

I'm weighing the typing cost of a wet-ink effect: decorations would wrap new text in spans and re-render the DOM around the caret, which could disturb IME and spellcheck. I'll check the typing-performance notes first. I'm also considering the CSS Custom Highlight API as a way to tint recent text without touching the DOM, though it only accepts a limited set of properties.

I'm checking whether highlight ranges can carry the wet-ink effect without touching the DOM, and I'm weighing a few ages of highlight that ranges move through as they dry.

Next I'm working through the drying steps for the wet-ink effect: the new range starts in the deepest ink tone, moves to a lighter one around 250ms, a third around 600ms, and is cleared at 1s. That staged fade would look like real drying, and it only needs a timer and some Range objects. I'm also checking how live Ranges behave when ProseMirror edits the text nodes under them.

I'm settling on the save state as the wet-to-dry link: ink stays wet until the local persist flush completes, then blots dry, so the saved state shows on the words themselves. I'm weighing whether the wet-ink colour would distract a writer, so I'm leaning toward a very subtle tint, a blue-black close to the manuscript's ink. Iron-gall ink goes on blue-black and oxidises to brown-black over time, so starting the typed text bluish and letting it settle into the normal ink would be historically grounded.

The blue-black ink idea works well for typing, since it's legible and low-chroma. I'm also considering a vermilion caret, which would be a cheap way to give the editor its own identity, like a red pencil marking the place.

I'm weighing a vermilion caret against a custom smooth caret overlay: the overlay would need coordinates on every keystroke and could add latency, so I'm leaning toward keeping the native caret and just tinting it vermilion.

I'm thinking of a thin vermilion tick in the left margin that glides to whichever line the caret is on, a reading guide that shows position without touching the text. I'm sketching a mouse-driven idea where a soft desk-lamp light follows the pointer across the page, and I'm weighing whether it should stay just a subtle wash so it doesn't pull attention from the text.

I can do this with a CSS radial gradient that follows the pointer, updated through CSS custom properties and throttled to animation frames, on a separate composited layer so it doesn't touch the text. A WebGL shader would be heavier on integrated graphics, and blend modes over text could force costly compositing, so the layered gradient looks like the cheaper route.

I'm thinking through how the paper could react to the pointer: a soft lamp-like light drifting across the page, moved with a cheap transform on its own layer behind the text. I'm weighing whether a desk-lamp light that follows the pointer would be decorative or actually useful. I'm weighing a zen-mode idea where a lamp held near the pointer reveals the editors' pencil marks, like raking light showing indentations in paper, so the notes stay hidden until wanted. The catch is that CSS can't measure distance per element, so I'd need JavaScript to check mark positions against the pointer, probably using cached rects that get refreshed on scroll, resize, or document changes.

I'm going through the candidate ideas and their trade-offs, weighing which are worth building. Scrolling is next: a vermilion mark on the masthead rule could track reading progress, like a bookmark ribbon, driven by a scroll-linked animation on the manuscript scroller.

I'm thinking about a bookmark-style ribbon for reading progress, like a vermilion silk ribbon that hangs from the top and lengthens as you scroll, using a scroll-linked animation on the manuscript scroller.

Now I'm weighing a thin vermilion ribbon hanging from the top-right corner of the page, the way a book's ribbon marker would, lengthening as the reader scrolls. I'm dropping parallax on the page sheets, since it would be distracting during long reading. Now I'm moving on to dragging: section handles could get a vermilion galley-rule drop indicator in place of the purple one, with the dragged section shown as a galley slip. <result>I've written the report below with a source URL on each bullet. Some details I couldn't confirm are flagged inline and collected in the last section.

## Research report: interaction motion for Twyne

### 1. Game feel and juice applied to productivity UI
- **Juice it or lose it (Jonasson and Purho, GDC 2012).** They take a plain Breakout and keep the rules fixed. They then add layers in order: colour, tweening and easing, squash and stretch, sound, particles, screen shake, then faces. Takeaway: feedback comes in layers on top of rules that don't change, so juice is presentation and never changes outcomes. https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016487/juice-it-or-lose
- **Screen shake causes motion sickness.** Later write-ups say "a shake should be a punch, not an earthquake." Shake a stamp, never the viewport. https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016487/juice-it-or-lose (Nijman's "Art of Screenshake" talk covers the same ground)
- **Emil Kowalski: animation budget scales with how often an action happens.** Rules from his STANDARDS.md:
  - Used 100+ times a day: no animation.
  - Used tens of times a day: remove or minimise.
  - Occasional (modals, toasts): a standard animation.
  - Rare (onboarding, celebrations): delight is allowed.
  - Keyboard-triggered actions are never animated. Raycast is his example.
  https://github.com/emilkowalski/skills/blob/main/skills/review-animations/STANDARDS.md
- **Kowalski's numbers.**
  - UI animations stay under 300ms. 200ms is the default.
  - Press feedback is 100–160ms, for example `transform 160ms ease-out` with scale 0.97.
  - Tooltips take 125ms, and every tooltip after the first shows instantly.
  - Drawers take about 500ms with `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`.
  - Stagger items by 30–80ms.
  - Use ease-out for entering elements and avoid ease-in, which feels slow.
  - Use blur (around 2px) only as a last resort to smooth a crossfade.
  https://emilkowal.ski/ui/7-practical-animation-tips
- **Rauno Freiberg, "Invisible details of interaction design".**
  - Motion should be interruptible: you can reverse it mid-gesture and never have to wait for it to finish.
  - Thrown objects keep their momentum, and bounce matches how heavy the object should feel.
  - A threshold commits an action. Before the threshold, the response tracks the input.
  - "Fidgetability" means small satisfying responses invite people to repeat them.
  - Scroll stays with the pane where it started.
  Takeaway: margin notes and stamps should be draggable and reversible before they commit. https://rauno.me/craft/interaction-design
- **Linear's timing.** This comes from a third-party reading of Linear's stylesheet, not from Linear itself. Highlights fade in over 0s and out over 0.15s. The quick, regular and slow transitions are 0.1s, 0.25s and 0.35s. Popovers appear instantly and fade out on dismiss. Width, height and margin are never animated. Takeaway: appear instantly, leave softly. https://performance.dev/how-is-linear-so-fast-a-technical-breakdown
- **Raycast's bar is "feeling native".** Their deep dive lists: no flicker when views appear, no `cursor: pointer` on controls, and the WebView finishes drawing before the window is shown. https://www.raycast.com/blog/a-technical-deep-dive-into-the-new-raycast
- **Apple HIG.** Avoid motion on UI interactions people repeat often. Avoid oscillation near 0.2 Hz (one cycle every five seconds); if something must oscillate, keep the amplitude low and the content translucent. This matters for any "breathing" idle state. https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion
- **Vercel interface guidelines.**
  - Animate only `transform` and `opacity`, and never use `transition: all`.
  - Every animation must be interruptible.
  - Motion that autoplays for more than 5 seconds needs a pause control.
  - Decorative loops stop under reduced motion.
  - Per-keystroke work must stay cheap.
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines/main/command.md

### 2. Editors with a distinctive typing, caret or scroll feel
- **Word's gliding caret (since Office 2013) is widely disliked.**
  - On Hacker News: "that cursor animation is just awful… laggy animation on top of what should be instant."
  - Word's own "Provide feedback with animation" checkbox doesn't turn it off. The only fixes are the Windows-wide animation setting (which some Windows updates turn back on) or the `DisableAnimations` registry value.
  Takeaway: never delay the caret on a keypress. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19686799
- **VS Code keeps the caret instant while typing.** `editor.cursorSmoothCaretAnimation` has the values off, explicit and on. "explicit" animates only when you jump with a click or navigation, not while typing. Adopt that split. https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/169332
- **Monkeytype** has `smoothCaret: off | slow | medium | fast`, and the speed setting came from users saying the glide was too slow. Typing-test users accept a smooth caret only when it is fast and optional. Source for the options: https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype (packages/schemas/src/configs.ts). Source for the complaint: https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype/discussions/1248
- **iA Writer's Focus Mode** dims everything except the current sentence or paragraph, and Typewriter Mode keeps the current line vertically centred. Both are toggles, and the dimming is a colour change, not movement. https://ia.net/writer/support/editor/focus-mode
- **Ulysses, Typora, Obsidian, Bear.**
  - Ulysses' typewriter mode, with a configurable line position and a line highlight, is a fan favourite.
  - Typora has Focus (F8) and Typewriter (F9) modes.
  - Obsidian gets the same through the obsidian-typewriter-mode plugin, which offers line position as a percentage, a highlight style and paragraph dimming.
  - Bear users still have an open feature request for typewriter mode.
  Takeaway: writers value stillness and a predictable eye line more than motion. Unverified: Ulysses' exact options, because its help page now redirects.
- **Paper by FiftyThree (now WeTransfer)** drew stroke width from drawing speed rather than pressure, on a custom OpenGL engine; a later update advertised three-times-faster ink. A strong precedent for ink whose physics comes from speed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FiftyThree
- **Teenage Engineering's OP-1** gives each mode its own colour and animated graphic, so the playful visuals tell you which mode you are in. https://blakecrosley.com/guides/design/teenage-engineering
- **Not verified:** Craft's and Hemingway's motion. Hemingway uses static colour highlights only.

### 3. Ink, paper and letterpress on the web
- **SVG filter recipes for type (Carmen Ansio).**
  - Ink gain: `feMorphology dilate`, then `feFlood`, then `feComposite in`.
  - Rough, bled edges: `feTurbulence` into `feDisplacementMap`. `fractalNoise` gives softer edges than `turbulence`.
  - Pitfalls: turbulence, displacement and lighting are the expensive primitives. Defs inside a `display:none` SVG are dropped in Chromium. Set `color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"`. CSS cannot animate filter primitive attributes, so drive changes from JS with requestAnimationFrame and an IntersectionObserver.
  https://www.carmenansio.com/articles/svg-filters-on-type/
- **SVG filter performance.**
  - Keep the filter region tight. `feTurbulence` is unbounded and defaults to a region of 120%.
  - Never animate transform on a filtered element, because the filter is recomputed every frame.
  - Pre-render the result to a bitmap.
  - CSS filter functions are much cheaper than SVG filters.
  Rule for Twyne: never put a live filter on the editor surface. Use filters only on small, short-lived elements such as a stamp. https://tympanus.net/codrops/2019/02/19/svg-filter-effects-creating-texture-with-feturbulence/
- **Paper grain.** Generate the texture once (feTurbulence or a shader) and cache it as a tiled background. Lighting by a moving light is best done as a fragment shader on a small canvas behind the text, at half or quarter resolution, re-rendered only when the light moves. I found no authoritative procedural paper shader; three.js normal-map approaches exist. https://discourse.threejs.org/t/distorted-grainy-material-due-to-a-normal-map/72599
- **Risograph and halftone.** Codrops has a risograph grain tutorial. glsl-halftone provides rotated dot grids. Mis-registration is a UV offset per spot-ink layer, which suits two inks, vermilion and cobalt.
  - https://tympanus.net/codrops/2022/03/07/creating-a-risograph-grain-light-effect-in-three-js/
  - https://github.com/glslify/glsl-halftone
- **Letterpress deboss in CSS** is a pair of `text-shadow` layers: light offset down, dark offset up. Animating the pair fakes a moving light. Note that `text-shadow` does not render on `background-clip:text`.
- **`backdrop-filter`** is costly inside scrolling content. I found no benchmark. Avoid it over the manuscript.

### 4. Browser APIs (verified November 2026)
- **CSS Custom Highlight API.** Baseline Newly Available since 2026-03-24 (Chrome 105, Safari 17.2, Firefox 149).
  - Allowed properties: `color`, `background-color`, `text-decoration*`, `text-shadow`, `-webkit-text-stroke/fill`.
  - `background-image` is ignored.
  - There are no transitions or animations today. On 2026-10-30 the CSSWG resolved that highlights should get opacity and that animations and transitions should be allowed. That is spec intent and is not shipped.
  - To animate now, swap highlight names or change registered ranges from JS.
  - Sources: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/::highlight and https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/14613
- **Same-document View Transitions.** Baseline Newly Available since 2025-10-14, Firefox 144 last. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/view-transitions/
- **Scroll-driven animations.** Baseline Newly Available since 2026-10-27 (Chrome 115, Safari 26, Firefox 159). Older articles saying Firefox needs a flag are out of date. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/scroll-driven-animations/
- **`@property`.** Baseline since 2024-07 (Firefox 128 last). Safe for animated gradients and ink-fill progress. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/registered-custom-properties/
- **`linear()` easing.** Widely Available since 2026-06. Safe for spring curves in pure CSS. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/linear-easing/
- **Popover** is Baseline since 2025-01 and **`@starting-style`** since 2024-08. I found no separate support data for `popover=hint`.
  - https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/popover/
  - https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/starting-style/
- **`interpolate-size`** ships in Chromium only (129+). Firefox and Safari have not shipped it. Gate it with `@supports`. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/interpolate-size/
- **WebGPU.**
  - Chrome 113+ on Windows, macOS and ChromeOS. Android ships too; I didn't confirm the version.
  - Firefox 141 on Windows, and Firefox 145 on Apple Silicon macOS Tahoe.
  - Safari 26.
  - Linux Chrome is a gradual rollout on Vulkan, and Linux Firefox is Nightly only.
  - WebGL2 stays the default for ambient shaders, with WebGPU as an optional upgrade.
  - https://web.dev/blog/webgpu-supported-major-browsers
  - https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-webgpu-144 (I could not confirm the exact Linux GPU list.)

### 5. Motion that communicates consequence and trust
- **Undo beats "are you sure?"** People click through repeated warnings out of habit (Raskin). Gmail's Undo Send holds the message 5–30s. Use a visible delayed commit for "send to AI" or "publish". Keep heavy friction, like typing the item's name as GitHub does, for permanent destructive actions only. https://alistapart.com/article/neveruseawarning/
- **Hold-to-confirm.** Timings in component libraries range from 300ms to 2s. It is hard for people with tremor, so provide a single-activation path for keyboard and screen readers, and let releasing early cancel cleanly. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pointer-cancellation.html
- **Disabled-with-reason.** Use `aria-disabled` rather than `disabled` so the control stays focusable, and explain why it is disabled. This fits out-of-credits and rate-limited states.
  - https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2021/08/frustrating-design-patterns-disabled-buttons/
  - https://uxdesign.cc/never-ever-disable-buttons-requirements-for-an-accessible-solution-acaf9c5191f9
- **Response-time limits (NN/g).**
  - Under 0.1s feels instant and needs no feedback.
  - About 1s keeps the user's train of thought; a subtle indicator helps.
  - Over about 10s needs real progress, such as percent done.
  Map AI waits onto these bands. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/
- **AI thinking states.**
  - Accepted patterns: show the current step and total steps, an elapsed counter ("Thinking for N s"), steps that collapse, and a clear "done" state.
  - Anti-pattern: fake progress shown before the model has started.
  - Text shimmer is now a generic AI cliché.
  - A stronger fit for Twyne is to show what an editor is reading, for example a marker moving through the paragraphs it has consumed.
  - Source: https://panelui.dev/docs/ai-components/shimmer, a component library. I found no authoritative critique of shimmer.

### 6. Ambient life and accessibility
- **Smooth remote cursors.** Fit a spline through position updates (about every 50–80ms) instead of using CSS transitions, which never finish when updates arrive irregularly. This is perfect-cursors, used in tldraw. Use it for any AI-editor presence marker. https://github.com/steveruizok/perfect-cursors
- **Figma shows your own edits before the server confirms them** and ignores conflicting incoming changes until then, to avoid flicker. The same applies to local versus synced state. https://www.figma.com/blog/how-figmas-multiplayer-technology-works/
- **WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA).** Motion triggered by interaction must be possible to disable unless it is essential. Colour, blur and opacity changes don't count as motion, so a reduced-motion mode can keep fades and ink-colour shifts. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/animation-from-interactions.html
- **Vestibular triggers.** Parallax, scroll-jacking, zoom, spinning, and large or full-screen motion. Never use parallax or scroll-linked movement in the manuscript; scroll-driven effects belong in the margin or chrome only. https://alistapart.com/article/designing-safer-web-animation-for-motion-sensitivity/
- **Opt in to motion.** Josh Comeau and Ben Myers suggest motion only under `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`, plus an in-app override. https://benmyers.dev/encyclopedia/reduced-motion/
- **Time-of-day lighting.** Precedents are f.lux, Night Shift and dark mode by local sunlight (Hacker News, 2021). Change it slowly, never in steps, and keep text contrast fixed.

### What I couldn't verify
- Ulysses' exact typewriter-mode options (its help page redirected).
- Craft's motion behaviour.
- The exact GPU list for Chrome's WebGPU rollout on Linux.
- Kowalski's ease-out curve values other than the drawer curve.
- Linear's numbers are third-party, not from Linear.
- Apple HIG wording on "let people cancel" (not seen in the text I fetched).
- No benchmark for the cost of `backdrop-filter`.

### 10 gaps that fit a literary editor with AI editors
1. **A caret that never glides on a keystroke** but leaves a brief wet-ink fade on each new glyph, done with highlight colour (no layout) and drying in about 300ms.
2. **Ink colour that tells you where text lives:** fresh ink for local only, dried ink once synced, a cobalt edge on text sent to a provider, and vermilion for published.
3. **Reading-progress presence for AI editors:** a quiet marker moving through the paragraphs each editor has read, with spline smoothing, instead of a shimmer or spinner.
4. **The rubric stamp:** a short ink-impression stamp with a halftone or mis-registration shader on a small canvas. It can be dragged and reversed until a threshold, and is fully undoable.
5. **"Send to the room" as a visible delayed commit:** the envelope sits on the desk for N seconds, and you can pull it back.
6. **Out-of-credits as an empty inkwell:** the control stays focusable and says why and when the credits refill.
7. **Margin notes that slide in from the margin edge,** grouped, with a stagger of 50ms or less. They never shift the manuscript layout.
8. **Paper grain lit by the time of day:** one cached texture plus a low-resolution light pass that only re-renders when the light changes. It pauses while you type.
9. **Destructive actions as a press imprint that deepens while held,** with a keyboard path and an undo window, rather than a modal.
10. **A Desk page where stats are set like a printer's composing stick:** movement happens only when you open the page, never during writing, and scroll effects stay out of the reading column.</result>

I'm now going through the seven surfaces to cover: the consequence grammar for local, synced, AI, publish and destructive actions, plus one or two gated shaders, a paper-fibre light and a stamp for grading, kept quiet during flow and off under reduced motion.

I'm working out the identity for the Press Room: everything is paper and ink, and each action borrows a step from the print shop. Typing should give newly written words a wet-ink sheen that dries over a moment. I'm weighing a CSS Custom Highlight approach for that, since per-keystroke decorations could cost too much.

I'm working out how the wet-ink effect can run without touching the DOM on every keystroke: the CSS Highlight API lets me update ranges in an animation frame instead of through ProseMirror transactions. Highlights can't transition, so I'm considering stepped drying, moving recent ranges through a few highlight tiers on a timer, rather than animating a custom property that all wet ranges would share.

I'm working out how to keep the typed-word shimmer cheap: each keystroke only needs a live DOM range over the newly inserted characters, which the CSS Highlight API can colour without touching ProseMirror. Since these ranges survive ordinary in-place text edits, I'll only need to care when a re-render replaces the nodes, and then the range just collapses harmlessly.

I'm weighing whether the wet-ink colour should be a deeper, glossier shade of the ink colour, since fresh ink reads blacker and matte-brown as it dries, and I'll keep the change gentle enough to read as a colour fade rather than movement.

I'm checking whether text-shadow works inside ::highlight in Chromium, since that would give the wet-ink sheen. I'm also weighing a cobalt-black ink that starts bluer and dries toward brown-black, which fits the fountain-pen idea I'm building toward.

I'm settling on iron gall ink as the identity: freshly typed words would start faintly blue-black and darken into the manuscript ink over about 1.2 seconds, the way that ink oxidises. It stays legible throughout, and the recency trail also helps when the eyes return to the page after looking away.

I'm weighing whether the wet-ink fade should be tied to the local save rather than a fixed timer: the ink stays blue until IndexedDB confirms the write, then dries. The catch is that saves can lag up to 2.5 seconds during continuous typing, which would actually read as "pending save," so that might be a feature rather than a bug.

I'm settling on a red caret for the manuscript, a deliberate choice that stands out from the usual system caret, while keeping the native caret so IME and accessibility don't break.

I'm settling the caret question by mapping colours to roles: the writer's hand is blue-black iron gall ink, while the editors' marks are vermilion, so the caret should match the writer's ink rather than the red pencil.

I'm weighing whether the caret should stay native, since animating its position tends to feel laggy and many people switch that kind of effect off. I'm also checking whether `caret-shape` could give it a bit more character without touching the caret's behaviour.

I'm picturing a "desk lamp" for the background: a faint paper-fibre texture behind the page, lit by a soft light that trails the cursor with a heavy, springy lag and drifts back to a resting corner when the mouse goes still. The page column itself stays untouched so the text keeps its legibility.

I'm checking whether the page background is transparent, since if it is, a faint raking light over the paper grain could sit under the text without hurting legibility. I'm also thinking about a shader at reduced resolution, rendering only while the lamp is moving, to keep the cost down.

I'm sketching the paper-grain lamp as a precomputed normal map sampled each frame and lit from the cursor position, rendered only while the light is still moving so it stays cheap on integrated graphics.

I'm weighing whether the lamp should be decorative at all, since the brief warns against UI that competes with the manuscript, so it has to stay very subtle and actually do something. The idea is that its light pools where the pointer is and brightens whichever margin card is under it, and perhaps it could signal when the AI editors are reading, though I'm wary of that becoming a gimmick. On the buttons themselves, hovering "Get notes" might preview the consequence, like a small chip showing what it sends.
