<result>I've written the report below with a source URL on each bullet. Some details I couldn't confirm are flagged inline and collected in the last section.

## Research report: interaction motion for Twyne

### 1. Game feel and juice applied to productivity UI
- **Juice it or lose it (Jonasson and Purho, GDC 2012).** They take a plain Breakout and keep the rules fixed. They then add layers in order: colour, tweening and easing, squash and stretch, sound, particles, screen shake, then faces. Takeaway: feedback comes in layers on top of rules that don't change, so juice is presentation and never changes outcomes. https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016487/juice-it-or-lose
- **Screen shake causes motion sickness.** Later write-ups say "a shake should be a punch, not an earthquake." Shake a stamp, never the viewport. https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016487/juice-it-or-lose (Nijman's "Art of Screenshake" talk covers the same ground)
- **Emil Kowalski: animation budget scales with how often an action happens.** Rules from his STANDARDS.md:
  - Used 100+ times a day: no animation.
  - Used tens of times a day: remove or minimise.
  - Occasional (modals, toasts): a standard animation.
  - Rare (onboarding, celebrations): delight is allowed.
  - Keyboard-triggered actions are never animated. Raycast is his example.
  https://github.com/emilkowalski/skills/blob/main/skills/review-animations/STANDARDS.md
- **Kowalski's numbers.**
  - UI animations stay under 300ms. 200ms is the default.
  - Press feedback is 100–160ms, for example `transform 160ms ease-out` with scale 0.97.
  - Tooltips take 125ms, and every tooltip after the first shows instantly.
  - Drawers take about 500ms with `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`.
  - Stagger items by 30–80ms.
  - Use ease-out for entering elements and avoid ease-in, which feels slow.
  - Use blur (around 2px) only as a last resort to smooth a crossfade.
  https://emilkowal.ski/ui/7-practical-animation-tips
- **Rauno Freiberg, "Invisible details of interaction design".**
  - Motion should be interruptible: you can reverse it mid-gesture and never have to wait for it to finish.
  - Thrown objects keep their momentum, and bounce matches how heavy the object should feel.
  - A threshold commits an action. Before the threshold, the response tracks the input.
  - "Fidgetability" means small satisfying responses invite people to repeat them.
  - Scroll stays with the pane where it started.
  Takeaway: margin notes and stamps should be draggable and reversible before they commit. https://rauno.me/craft/interaction-design
- **Linear's timing.** This comes from a third-party reading of Linear's stylesheet, not from Linear itself. Highlights fade in over 0s and out over 0.15s. The quick, regular and slow transitions are 0.1s, 0.25s and 0.35s. Popovers appear instantly and fade out on dismiss. Width, height and margin are never animated. Takeaway: appear instantly, leave softly. https://performance.dev/how-is-linear-so-fast-a-technical-breakdown
- **Raycast's bar is "feeling native".** Their deep dive lists: no flicker when views appear, no `cursor: pointer` on controls, and the WebView finishes drawing before the window is shown. https://www.raycast.com/blog/a-technical-deep-dive-into-the-new-raycast
- **Apple HIG.** Avoid motion on UI interactions people repeat often. Avoid oscillation near 0.2 Hz (one cycle every five seconds); if something must oscillate, keep the amplitude low and the content translucent. This matters for any "breathing" idle state. https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion
- **Vercel interface guidelines.**
  - Animate only `transform` and `opacity`, and never use `transition: all`.
  - Every animation must be interruptible.
  - Motion that autoplays for more than 5 seconds needs a pause control.
  - Decorative loops stop under reduced motion.
  - Per-keystroke work must stay cheap.
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines/main/command.md

### 2. Editors with a distinctive typing, caret or scroll feel
- **Word's gliding caret (since Office 2013) is widely disliked.**
  - On Hacker News: "that cursor animation is just awful… laggy animation on top of what should be instant."
  - Word's own "Provide feedback with animation" checkbox doesn't turn it off. The only fixes are the Windows-wide animation setting (which some Windows updates turn back on) or the `DisableAnimations` registry value.
  Takeaway: never delay the caret on a keypress. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19686799
- **VS Code keeps the caret instant while typing.** `editor.cursorSmoothCaretAnimation` has the values off, explicit and on. "explicit" animates only when you jump with a click or navigation, not while typing. Adopt that split. https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/169332
- **Monkeytype** has `smoothCaret: off | slow | medium | fast`, and the speed setting came from users saying the glide was too slow. Typing-test users accept a smooth caret only when it is fast and optional. Source for the options: https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype (packages/schemas/src/configs.ts). Source for the complaint: https://github.com/monkeytypegame/monkeytype/discussions/1248
- **iA Writer's Focus Mode** dims everything except the current sentence or paragraph, and Typewriter Mode keeps the current line vertically centred. Both are toggles, and the dimming is a colour change, not movement. https://ia.net/writer/support/editor/focus-mode
- **Ulysses, Typora, Obsidian, Bear.**
  - Ulysses' typewriter mode, with a configurable line position and a line highlight, is a fan favourite.
  - Typora has Focus (F8) and Typewriter (F9) modes.
  - Obsidian gets the same through the obsidian-typewriter-mode plugin, which offers line position as a percentage, a highlight style and paragraph dimming.
  - Bear users still have an open feature request for typewriter mode.
  Takeaway: writers value stillness and a predictable eye line more than motion. Unverified: Ulysses' exact options, because its help page now redirects.
- **Paper by FiftyThree (now WeTransfer)** drew stroke width from drawing speed rather than pressure, on a custom OpenGL engine; a later update advertised three-times-faster ink. A strong precedent for ink whose physics comes from speed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FiftyThree
- **Teenage Engineering's OP-1** gives each mode its own colour and animated graphic, so the playful visuals tell you which mode you are in. https://blakecrosley.com/guides/design/teenage-engineering
- **Not verified:** Craft's and Hemingway's motion. Hemingway uses static colour highlights only.

### 3. Ink, paper and letterpress on the web
- **SVG filter recipes for type (Carmen Ansio).**
  - Ink gain: `feMorphology dilate`, then `feFlood`, then `feComposite in`.
  - Rough, bled edges: `feTurbulence` into `feDisplacementMap`. `fractalNoise` gives softer edges than `turbulence`.
  - Pitfalls: turbulence, displacement and lighting are the expensive primitives. Defs inside a `display:none` SVG are dropped in Chromium. Set `color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"`. CSS cannot animate filter primitive attributes, so drive changes from JS with requestAnimationFrame and an IntersectionObserver.
  https://www.carmenansio.com/articles/svg-filters-on-type/
- **SVG filter performance.**
  - Keep the filter region tight. `feTurbulence` is unbounded and defaults to a region of 120%.
  - Never animate transform on a filtered element, because the filter is recomputed every frame.
  - Pre-render the result to a bitmap.
  - CSS filter functions are much cheaper than SVG filters.
  Rule for Twyne: never put a live filter on the editor surface. Use filters only on small, short-lived elements such as a stamp. https://tympanus.net/codrops/2019/02/19/svg-filter-effects-creating-texture-with-feturbulence/
- **Paper grain.** Generate the texture once (feTurbulence or a shader) and cache it as a tiled background. Lighting by a moving light is best done as a fragment shader on a small canvas behind the text, at half or quarter resolution, re-rendered only when the light moves. I found no authoritative procedural paper shader; three.js normal-map approaches exist. https://discourse.threejs.org/t/distorted-grainy-material-due-to-a-normal-map/72599
- **Risograph and halftone.** Codrops has a risograph grain tutorial. glsl-halftone provides rotated dot grids. Mis-registration is a UV offset per spot-ink layer, which suits two inks, vermilion and cobalt.
  - https://tympanus.net/codrops/2022/03/07/creating-a-risograph-grain-light-effect-in-three-js/
  - https://github.com/glslify/glsl-halftone
- **Letterpress deboss in CSS** is a pair of `text-shadow` layers: light offset down, dark offset up. Animating the pair fakes a moving light. Note that `text-shadow` does not render on `background-clip:text`.
- **`backdrop-filter`** is costly inside scrolling content. I found no benchmark. Avoid it over the manuscript.

### 4. Browser APIs (verified November 2026)
- **CSS Custom Highlight API.** Baseline Newly Available since 2026-03-24 (Chrome 105, Safari 17.2, Firefox 149).

- **Hold-to-confirm.** Timings in component libraries range from 300ms to 2s. It is hard for people with tremor, so provide a single-activation path for keyboard and screen readers, and let releasing early cancel cleanly. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pointer-cancellation.html
- **Disabled-with-reason.** Use `aria-disabled` rather than `disabled` so the control stays focusable, and explain why it is disabled. This fits out-of-credits and rate-limited states.
  - https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2021/08/frustrating-design-patterns-disabled-buttons/
  - https://uxdesign.cc/never-ever-disable-buttons-requirements-for-an-accessible-solution-acaf9c5191f9
- **Response-time limits (NN/g).**
  - Under 0.1s feels instant and needs no feedback.
  - About 1s keeps the user's train of thought; a subtle indicator helps.
  - Over about 10s needs real progress, such as percent done.
  Map AI waits onto these bands. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/
- **AI thinking states.**
  - Accepted patterns: show the current step and total steps, an elapsed counter ("Thinking for N s"), steps that collapse, and a clear "done" state.
  - Anti-pattern: fake progress shown before the model has started.
  - Text shimmer is now a generic AI cliché.
  - A stronger fit for Twyne is to show what an editor is reading, for example a marker moving through the paragraphs it has consumed.
  - Source: https://panelui.dev/docs/ai-components/shimmer, a component library. I found no authoritative critique of shimmer.

- **Smooth remote cursors.** Fit a spline through position updates (about every 50–80ms) instead of using CSS transitions, which never finish when updates arrive irregularly. This is perfect-cursors, used in tldraw. Use it for any AI-editor presence marker. https://github.com/steveruizok/perfect-cursors

Colour, blur and opacity changes don't count as motion, so a reduced-motion mode can keep fades and ink-colour shifts. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/animation-from-interactions.html
- **Vestibular triggers.** Parallax, scroll-jacking, zoom, spinning, and large or full-screen motion. 2. **Ink colour that tells you where text lives:** fresh ink for local only, dried ink once synced, a cobalt edge on text sent to a provider, and vermilion for published.

4. **The rubric stamp:** a short ink-impression stamp with a halftone or mis-registration shader on a small canvas. It can be dragged and reversed until a threshold, and is fully undoable.
5. **"Send to the room" as a visible delayed commit:** the envelope sits on the desk for N seconds, and you can pull it back.
6. **Out-of-credits as an empty inkwell:** the control stays focusable and says why and when the credits refill.

8. **Paper grain lit by the time of day:** one cached texture plus a low-resolution light pass that only re-renders when the light changes. It pauses while you type.
9. **Destructive actions as a press imprint that deepens while held,** with a keyboard path and an undo window, rather than a modal.
10. **A Desk page where stats are set like a printer's composing stick:** movement happens only when you open the page, never during writing, and scroll effects stay out of the reading column.</result>

## Research report: interaction motion for Twyne

### 1. Game feel and juice applied to productivity UI
- **Juice it or lose it (Jonasson and Purho, GDC 2012).** They take a plain Breakout and keep the rules fixed. They then add layers in order: colour, tweening and easing, squash and stretch, sound, particles, screen shake, then faces. Takeaway: feedback comes in layers on top of rules that don't change, so juice is presentation and never changes outcomes. https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016487/juice-it-or-lose
- **Screen shake causes motion sickness.** Later write-ups say "a shake should be a punch, not an earthquake." Shake a stamp, never the viewport. https://www.gdcvault.com/play/1016487/juice-it-or-lose (Nijman's "Art of Screenshake" talk covers the same ground)
- **Emil Kowalski: animation budget scales with how often an action happens.** Rules from his STANDARDS.md:
  - Used 100+ times a day: no animation.
  - Used tens of times a day: remove or minimise.
  - Occasional (modals, toasts): a standard animation.
  - Rare (onboarding, celebrations): delight is allowed.
  - Keyboard-triggered actions are never animated. Raycast is his example.
  https://github.com/emilkowalski/skills/blob/main/skills/review-animations/STANDARDS.md
- **Kowalski's numbers.**
  - UI animations stay under 300ms. 200ms is the default.
  - Press feedback is 100–160ms, for example `transform 160ms ease-out` with scale 0.97.
  - Tooltips take 125ms, and every tooltip after the first shows instantly.
  - Drawers take about 500ms with `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`.
  - Stagger items by 30–80ms.
  - Use ease-out for entering elements and avoid ease-in, which feels slow.
  - Use blur (around 2px) only as a last resort to smooth a crossfade.
  https://emilkowal.ski/ui/7-practical-animation-tips
- **Rauno Freiberg, "Invisible details of interaction design".**
  - Motion should be interruptible: you can reverse it mid-gesture and never have to wait for it to finish.
  - Thrown objects keep their momentum, and bounce matches how heavy the object should feel.
  - A threshold commits an action. Before the threshold, the response tracks the input.
  - "Fidgetability" means small satisfying responses invite people to repeat them.
  - Scroll stays with the pane where it started.
  Takeaway: margin notes and stamps should be draggable and reversible before they commit. https://rauno.me/craft/interaction-design
- **Linear's timing.** This comes from a third-party reading of Linear's stylesheet, not from Linear itself. Highlights fade in over 0s and out over 0.15s. The quick, regular and slow transitions are 0.1s, 0.25s and 0.35s. Popovers appear instantly and fade out on dismiss. Width, height and margin are never animated. Takeaway: appear instantly, leave softly. https://performance.dev/how-is-linear-so-fast-a-technical-breakdown
- **Raycast's bar is "feeling native".** Their deep dive lists: no flicker when views appear, no `cursor: pointer` on controls, and the WebView finishes drawing before the window is shown. https://www.raycast.com/blog/a-technical-deep-dive-into-the-new-raycast
- **Apple HIG.** Avoid motion on UI interactions people repeat often. Avoid oscillation near 0.2 Hz (one cycle every five seconds); if something must oscillate, keep the amplitude low and the content translucent. This matters for any "breathing" idle state. https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion
- **Vercel interface guidelines.**
  - Animate only `transform` and `opacity`, and never use `transition: all`.
  - Every animation must be interruptible.
  - Motion that autoplays for more than 5 seconds needs a pause control.
  - Decorative loops stop under reduced motion.
  - Per-keystroke work must stay cheap.
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines/main/command.md

- **Word's gliding caret (since Office 2013) is widely disliked.**
  - On Hacker News: "that cursor animation is just awful… laggy animation on top of what should be instant."
  - Word's own "Provide feedback with animation" checkbox doesn't turn it off. The only fixes are the Windows-wide animation setting (which some Windows updates turn back on) or the `DisableAnimations` registry value.
  Takeaway: never delay the caret on a keypress. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19686799
- **VS Code keeps the caret instant while typing.** `editor.cursorSmoothCaretAnimation` has the values off, explicit and on. "explicit" animates only when you jump with a click or navigation, not while typing. Adopt that split. https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/169332
- **Monkeytype** has `smoothCaret: off | slow | medium | fast`, and the speed setting came from users saying the glide was too slow. - **Ulysses, Typora, Obsidian, Bear.**
  - Ulysses' typewriter mode, with a configurable line position and a line highlight, is a fan favourite.
  - Typora has Focus (F8) and Typewriter (F9) modes.

- **SVG filter recipes for type (Carmen Ansio).**
  - Ink gain: `feMorphology dilate`, then `feFlood`, then `feComposite in`.
  - Rough, bled edges: `feTurbulence` into `feDisplacementMap`. `fractalNoise` gives softer edges than `turbulence`.

  https://www.carmenansio.com/articles/svg-filters-on-type/

  - Never animate transform on a filtered element, because the filter is recomputed every frame.
  - Pre-render the result to a bitmap.
  - CSS filter functions are much cheaper than SVG filters.

  - https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/popover/
  - https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/starting-style/
- **`interpolate-size`** ships in Chromium only (129+). Firefox and Safari have not shipped it. Gate it with `@supports`. https://web-platform-dx.github.io/web-features-explorer/features/interpolate-size/
- **WebGPU.**
  - Chrome 113+ on Windows, macOS and ChromeOS. Android ships too; I didn't confirm the version.
  - Firefox 141 on Windows, and Firefox 145 on Apple Silicon macOS Tahoe.
  - Safari 26.
  - Linux Chrome is a gradual rollout on Vulkan, and Linux Firefox is Nightly only.
  - WebGL2 stays the default for ambient shaders, with WebGPU as an optional upgrade.
  - https://web.dev/blog/webgpu-supported-major-browsers
  - https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-webgpu-144 (I could not confirm the exact Linux GPU list.)

  - https://uxdesign.cc/never-ever-disable-buttons-requirements-for-an-accessible-solution-acaf9c5191f9
- **Response-time limits (NN/g).**
  - Under 0.1s feels instant and needs no feedback.
  - About 1s keeps the user's train of thought; a subtle indicator helps.
  - Over about 10s needs real progress, such as percent done.
  Map AI waits onto these bands. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/
- **AI thinking states.**
  - Accepted patterns: show the current step and total steps, an elapsed counter ("Thinking for N s"), steps that collapse, and a clear "done" state.
  - Anti-pattern: fake progress shown before the model has started.
  - Text shimmer is now a generic AI cliché.
  - A stronger fit for Twyne is to show what an editor is reading, for example a marker moving through the paragraphs it has consumed.
  - Source: https://panelui.dev/docs/ai-components/shimmer, a component library. I found no authoritative critique of shimmer.

The save chain runs from the 500ms derive debounce, capped at 2.5s, through the content event and the 400ms local persist into IndexedDB, which then emits the draft-saved event. After a pause, the ink should dry roughly a second after the last keystroke, but during continuous typing I'm still working out how the 2.5s cap and the 400ms persist delay interact.

Persist fires 400ms after each derive, so during continuous typing the wet tail stays short, roughly 2.9 seconds of text, and dries in waves every 2.5 seconds. If two content events land before a persist, only the latest HTML is saved, so the draft-saved event covers everything up to the latest cutoff, and that's the point to dry ranges up to.

I'm weighing whether to accept a rare race: a content event could land between the IDB write starting and committing, so the saved HTML would be older than the latest cutoff and those ranges would dry about 400ms early. Recording cutoffs in a sequence and matching them to the flushed HTML would be exact, but the window is only about 10-50ms, so I'm leaning toward accepting it. I still need to check whether the route's contentHandler only saves on certain changes.

I'm weighing a fallback for when saves never report back: either keep the ink wet as an honest signal that something failed, or cap how many wet ranges can pile up so the page doesn't slow down.

I'm checking whether shared mode or a read-only session ever dispatches `twyne:draft-saved`, since otherwise the ink would stay wet indefinitely. My plan is a fallback: if no save acknowledgement arrives within about 6 seconds of a content event, I'll dry the ink on a short timer instead.

Now I'm settling the visual stages: the wet ink gets a glossy glow, and on drying it steps through two lighter tints over about 330ms before clearing. Speech highlights should take priority over these wet-ink ranges, so I'll give the wet ink the lowest priority. I'm also keeping in mind that building ranges from DOM positions on every rebuild could get costly.

I'm checking whether the highlight painting itself triggers any relayout, since the wet-ink ranges would be painted on every keystroke.

Now I'm sketching the lamp effect: a canvas behind the text, sized at a lower resolution and scaled up, with a shader that builds a paper-fibre height field and lights it from a point above the desk that follows the pointer.

I'm sketching the lamp's temperature by time of day: cool daylight from the upper left in the morning, neutral in the afternoon, and a tighter, warmer tungsten pool in the evening. In the dark theme it should read as a reading lamp after hours, a bit warmer and more visible.

I'm now sketching how the lamp responds to the pointer: it follows the cursor only after a real move of more than 2px, pauses while typing, and drifts back to its resting pool over about 800ms when the pointer leaves the window. Reduced-motion users get a static lamp at the resting spot, and if WebGL is unavailable I'll fall back to a static CSS version.

I'm weighing where the lamp canvas should sit, since the editor's scroller has an opaque background that would hide anything placed behind it. One option is to put the canvas inside the scroller as a sticky element so it stays fixed while the text scrolls, and I'm still working out the sizing for that.

I'm working out how the lamp holder sits in the scroller: a sticky zero-height wrapper with a negative bottom margin, so it doesn't take up layout space. The open question is stacking order, since the page canvas needs to paint above the lamp while the sticky wrapper creates its own stacking context at z-index 0.

I'm working out whether the page canvas is opaque, since the lamp should only light the desk and not show through the sheet. The stacking order works out because the lamp holder comes earlier in the DOM than the page, so the page paints on top. What I still need to confirm is the page's background.

I'm checking whether the page canvas is transparent: if it is, the lamp light would show through beneath the text, which is fine as long as the ink stays dark. A very faint warm pool on the paper would read like raking light, not a loss of contrast.

I'm working out how the page canvas should sit over the lamp: the page area should only get a faint warm pool with no fibre texture, so the text stays crisp, while the desk around it gets the full paper-fibre texture lit by the lamp.

I'm picturing the desk as a sheet of laid paper with faint chain lines that only show up when the lamp rakes across them. A watermark could sit in there too, appearing only when the light passes near it, and it's a small hidden detail that's worth having.

I'm picturing the desk as a large sheet of laid paper, with fine laid lines and chain lines that only show under the lamp's raking light. A faint watermark could tile across it, revealed only where the light passes near it.

I'm settling on a lighter setup for the desk: a half-resolution shader with a few octaves of noise, chain lines, and a texture sample, which should stay cheap enough to run at 60fps and only needs to redraw when the pointer moves. I'm also mounting the lamp on the Desk page's background so it can slide across the ledger.

I'm picturing the desk's scroll behaviour now: a vermilion ribbon bookmark in the left margin whose length tracks reading progress, driven purely by CSS scroll timelines so it stays on the compositor. The page sheet itself will slide over the desk while the lamp pool stays anchored to the viewport.

The page canvas sits inside the scroller while the lamp canvas stays sticky to the viewport, so the desk texture holds still as the sheet slides across it. Pagination gaps would then reveal the stationary desk between pages. The ribbon bookmark is a scroll-linked element I'll leave for the manuscript lane to spec.

I'm listing the remaining identity hooks for the interface: the drop cursor on proofreader's caret, dragging the page ruler, file drag with crop marks, and section drag, all assigned to the manuscript lane. Hover and typing feedback stay in view too, with the word count left static on every keystroke and only a rare fleuron stamp at each hundred-word milestone.

I'm laying out the consequence grammar for interactions, starting with local-only actions, which I'll tie to a graphite pencil metaphor and muted ink colour across hover, press, busy and done states.

I'm laying out the interaction consequences in a table: local actions get a graphite-pencil treatment, sync gets a carbon-copy effect, and the provider case uses a postmark that shows where the text is going. The publish row is cut off at its start, so I'll wait for the rest before settling its treatment.

Next I'm splitting the work into parallel lanes, since everything touches one shared stylesheet and that would conflict if done in a single pass. I'm also planning a written motion spec with shared tokens and reusable primitives, and then per-component treatments with before-and-after captures so the choices can be compared.

I'm now sketching the motion language itself, giving it a name rooted in the Twyne identity of a writers' room and letterpress. The materials I'm drawing from are paper, ink, type, galley proofs, and pneumatic post. My core aim is a consequence grammar, where each kind of effect gets its own consistent physical metaphor so the interface shows what an action does.

Next I'm defining the "quiet" consequences first: local-only changes get a graphite treatment, a light, quick, reversible settle with no travel, and a faint underline sweep as feedback. Then comes the saved-to-disk case, where I'm considering wet ink that dries once the save lands in IndexedDB, so the save state shows up in the text being written. That's appealing, but per-keystroke decorations could be costly and could hurt readability, so I'm looking at using the Custom Highlight API to mark recently typed text with a subtle text-shadow instead of animating it.

Now I'm looking at how the "saved" state could show up in the text itself: newly typed words stay wet-looking until the save lands in IndexedDB, then they dry. Since highlights can't animate, I'd step through a few highlight variants over about 600ms, and that stays cheap because the Highlight API only touches paint, not layout. The open question is cost: tracking unsaved inserted ranges means mapping positions through every ProseMirror transaction, so I want to check that bookkeeping is affordable.

I'm checking whether the wet-ink idea stays readable: the color shift has to be subtle, something closer to fresh ink that's slightly richer than the page, so it reads as a state without pulling attention away from the words.

Iron gall ink starts out blue and darkens to black as it oxidizes, which makes it a fitting reference for a literary app. Fresh text could sit in a faintly blue-black tone and settle to ink-black once it's saved to disk, so the save state lives in the writing itself. Since it doesn't move anything or delay the caret, it fits the rule against slowing typing. The sync indicator can handle the Convex side.

I'm checking whether the highlight color would clobber any text color the writer picked, since the highlight pseudo-element applies over colored text. Using only a text-shadow or decoration might avoid that, so I'm weighing those options against each other. I'm also keeping in mind that the dark theme needs fresh ink mixed from theme variables, and that IME composition should skip updates.

I'm weighing whether a faint "wet" sheen on the text would look blurry, and settling on a plain color shift instead. Writer-chosen colors are rare, so a brief blue-black override on those few ranges until the save lands, roughly a second after the last keystroke, seems acceptable. I'm tracing the timing chain from the debounced derive through the local persist to the draft-saved event to confirm that window.

Now I'm thinking through the timing: during continuous typing the derive max-wait is 2.5s, so wet ink would dry in periodic waves behind the caret. But a save only covers text that existed when the snapshot was taken, so I'd need to mark the wet ranges at snapshot time and dry only those when the draft-saved event arrives.

I'm working out how the save snapshot ties into the dry step: the wet ranges should move into a sealed set when the content event fires, and only that sealed set should dry once the draft-saved event arrives. I'm also checking the handoff, since the editor dispatches content from the derive step and the route schedules a local persist about 400ms later, so the dry should follow that persist rather than the keystrokes.

Saved text would dry only once it's on disk, but a save covers only what existed at snapshot time, so timing matters. I'm weighing whether the dry step can be exact or whether a few hundred milliseconds of early drying on an in-flight write is acceptable, given the "saved means on disk" promise.

I'm weighing whether a save-timestamp could be added to the content event so the draft-saved signal can match the exact snapshot it acknowledges, which would keep the dry step honest about what is on disk. I'd also skip wet ink for remote collaborative edits and for content loaded in from storage, so only the writer's own typing gets the effect.

I'm considering the sync step as a separate, quieter moment: a small stamp-like tick on the sync dot when the account save lands, maybe with a brief ring, as a postal cancellation would mark a sent letter. That would keep the Convex side visible in the status bar without pulling focus from the page.

Now I'm working out the airmail-style marker for any action that sends text to an AI provider, using the cobalt and vermilion chevron edge as a visual signal that the text is leaving the desk.

Now I'm settling on an airmail-style marker for anything that sends text to an AI provider: a thin chevron border in the vermilion and cobalt of the palette that runs along the button edge on hover, with a small destination slip stating what gets sent and roughly what it costs. Once clicked, the chevron runs once quickly while the text is in transit, then turns into a postmark stamp when the reply lands, and the same cue would appear across the selection popover, Cast, Rubric, and comments so the consequence reads the same everywhere.

I'm wondering how the app could know, at render time, where a given piece of text will end up. The destination shows up in the same slip as the cost: a hosted room with credits, the user's own provider key, or a model running on the device. If it stays local, the button should drop the airmail edge and get a plain pencil mark instead.

I'm settling on the airmail-style marker for anything that sends text to a provider, and checking what the app can actually know about where a feature's text ends up. The hosted, own-key, and on-device cases would each get a different cue, so the button shows what happens before anyone clicks it.

Now I'm looking at the publish action: since it's rare, it can carry a bit more delight, like an ink-roller sweep across the share card ending in a stamp, marked with a halftone-dot edge to signal it goes to print.

I'm looking at destructive actions next, weighing an undo toast for local deletions against a hold-to-confirm strike for server-side ones like unpublishing or removing a collaborator, with a shared component that draws a vermilion rule across the button.

I'm laying out the rest of the consequence grammar: pencil for local reversible changes, ink for saves to this device, a carbon tick for account sync, airmail chevrons for anything sent to a provider, halftone dots for publishing, and a vermilion strike for destructive actions.

I'm settling on shared-checkout lanes rather than worktrees, since the user's uncommitted changes to the eslint plugin and related files would otherwise need committing around, and another thread may be working in this same tree. Each lane will stick to its own files and avoid any state-changing git.

I'm settling on how to build the motion system: I'll write the shared tokens and primitives first, and I'm working through which lane owns each large file so no two lanes edit the same one.

I'm working out how the editor's identity should read: it's a print shop or newsroom, with paper, ink, metal type, stamps, and pneumatic tubes, plus the room of persona editors leaving margin notes. The motion already leans into this, so the new layer should draw from those same physical materials.

I'm working out the consequence grammar next: each class of interaction needs its own motion language, so the user can read from the movement whether an action is safe to take or risky.

I'm sorting out the first consequence class: local edits that stay on this device and can be undone, which should feel like graphite on scratch paper, light and quick under about 120ms with no ceremony.

I'm defining the consequence for sending text off the device: a message leaves the desk in a sealed pneumatic capsule, and the control shows a perforated postage edge that signals the cost and destination before anyone clicks.

I'm defining the consequence for destructive actions as a spike: holding the control drives a copy spike up through the page, releasing early cancels it, and once it's done there's a brief window to pull it back out.

I'm sorting the consequence grammar into five verbs, each tied to a material and motion: pencil for local changes, ink for saves, post for anything sent off the desk that costs credits, press for publishing, and spike for destructive actions. Destructive actions like clearing the room, erasing a comment, or deleting history would all use the spike.

I'm laying out the consequence table next: each class of action gets a tell before it's taken, a press, a receipt afterward, a duration, and a color. The "post" row is the one I'm writing when it cuts off, where a perforated postage edge with the destination and cost appears on the control before anyone clicks, in cobalt.

I'm laying out the rest of the consequence table: the press row needs a vermilion proof edge and a register mark on the control, then a two-step make-ready-to-print with the platen coming down, leaving a debossed impression and a printed stamp as the receipt. The spike row is where I'm picking up, with a small hover reveal for destructive actions.

I'm sketching the spike row for destructive actions: a hover glyph under the item, then a hold that drives a progress line up through the button, with release cancelling it. Once spiked, the item drops onto the spike and fades, with an Unspike option for six seconds. Navigation stays a plain page turn, and I'm also thinking about how editors' presence should read while they work.

I'm now working out how the app can feel alive without distracting from the text: a faint warm lamp pool on the desk background that drifts slowly after the cursor, warmer in the evening, kept away from the manuscript and paused while typing.

I'm thinking through the ambient lamp glow: a faint warm radial gradient on a fixed layer that drifts after the cursor, kept off the manuscript and paused while typing. I'm weighing whether to use a blend mode or a plain low-opacity gradient, since a blend mode could be costly across the whole viewport.

I'm weighing a cursor-following lamp against the desk margins, since it could read as a generic spotlight effect in an editor. The question is whether the mouse should express the identity of the room, and I'm listing the options from there, starting with a desk lamp that follows the pointer.

I'm weighing whether the editors in the board should react to the cursor, since a glance from a persona portrait when you hover their note could feel alive, but turning faces toward the caret risks reading as creepy or gimmicky.

I'm weighing a reading ruler that follows the mouse in the left margin, a proofreader's line marker that shows which line is under the pointer, as a functional and on-theme alternative to a cursor-following light.

I'm considering a typing feedback idea: freshly typed characters would show as slightly glossier "wet" ink that dries back to normal over roughly 600 to 900 milliseconds. I'm weighing how to do that with the CSS Custom Highlight API, which avoids touching the DOM, though highlights can't animate on their own, so I'd have to cycle the recent ranges through a few staged highlight names.

I'm working out how to keep the wet-ink highlight ranges accurate, since ProseMirror may replace text nodes on each keystroke and leave stored Ranges stale. The plan is to recompute the ranges from tracked document positions at each drying step, mapped through transactions, rather than holding onto DOM references.

I'm weighing a wet-ink highlight with a slight sheen, since iron gall ink writes blue-grey and darkens to black as it oxidises, which would make the drying effect historically grounded. I'm also checking that the wet color stays legible against the page.

I'm pinning the wet-ink idea to a real rule: the ink is wet until the text is saved to disk, then it dries. The color shift is not motion, so it doesn't break the no-animation rule for keyboard actions, and it shouldn't slow the caret.

I'm settling on the "honest" version of the wet-ink idea: the ink stays wet until the draft actually reaches local storage, then dries, so the effect tells the truth about saving. The debounce timings mean it dries about a second after I stop typing and never lags more than roughly three seconds behind while I keep going. If the save fails, the ink stays wet, which is also useful as a visible warning.

I'm settling on a single "Liveliness" preference with three levels, Lively, Calm, and Still, stored in localStorage and applied as a data attribute on the root element, so the ambient lamp and idle motion can be turned off without touching functional motion. I'm also starting to think about the caret, since the research says it shouldn't animate on each keystroke.

I'm dropping the idea of typing sounds, since the app's existing audio cues would be overwhelmed by keystroke noise.

I'm laying down the motion foundation next: a small set of easing tokens in a motion stylesheet, a paper-style curve for sliding elements, a softer ink-settling curve, a heavier curve for the platen pressing down, and a slight-overshoot spring for slips landing.

Still writing the motion tokens, now the duration scale and the consequence colour mapping.

# eslint-plugin-qwik-guards

Shared ESLint guardrails for Qwik projects. The rules cover an empty-list
reconciliation path and plain-function JSX form wrappers, both of which have
caused fields to be replaced and lose focus in Twyne.

The empty-array runtime failure was reproduced on **Qwik 2.0.0-rc.4**. The form
wrapper rule covers a historical **Qwik 2 beta.42** failure, checked against the
actual source before and after its fix; that older runtime was not rerun during
plugin verification. Enable this preset deliberately in affected projects. It
does not detect your installed Qwik version or establish behavior on other
versions. It complements
`eslint-plugin-qwik` and does not replace it.

## Install in another project

Registry installation:

```sh
npm install --save-dev eslint-plugin-qwik-guards
```

The package is build-free ESM, has no runtime dependencies, and expects ESLint 9 and
Node 20.19 or newer. TypeScript projects keep their existing TypeScript ESLint
parser configuration.

To share a checkout or prerelease without a registry, produce a portable archive
from this package directory:

```sh
npm pack --pack-destination /tmp
```

In the target project:

```sh
npm install --save-dev /tmp/eslint-plugin-qwik-guards-0.1.0.tgz
```

Add the preset to the project's existing flat ESLint config, after its parser
configuration. Restrict `files` to the project's Qwik source roots if it contains
other frameworks:

```js
import qwikGuards from "eslint-plugin-qwik-guards";

export default [
  // Existing ESLint, Qwik, and TypeScript configurations go here.
  {
    ...qwikGuards.configs.recommended,
    files: ["src/**/*.{jsx,tsx}"],
  },
];
```

The preset enables `qwik-guards/no-empty-array-before-sibling` and
`qwik-guards/no-plain-jsx-form-wrapper` at `warn` severity.
To block merges after existing sites have been reviewed, override the rules to
`error` in a later config entry, or use ESLint's `--max-warnings 0` policy.

# eslint-plugin-qwik-guards

Shared ESLint guardrails for Qwik projects. The rules cover an empty-list
reconciliation path and plain-function JSX form wrappers, both of which have
caused fields to be replaced and lose focus in Twyne.

The empty-array runtime failure was reproduced on **Qwik 2.0.0-rc.4**. The form
wrapper rule covers a historical **Qwik 2 beta.42** failure, checked against the
actual source before and after its fix; that older runtime was not rerun during
plugin verification. Enable this preset deliberately in affected projects. It
does not detect your installed Qwik version or establish behavior on other
versions. It complements
`eslint-plugin-qwik` and does not replace it.

## Install in another project

Registry installation:

```sh
npm install --save-dev eslint-plugin-qwik-guards
```

The package is build-free ESM, has no runtime dependencies, and expects ESLint 9 and
Node 20.19 or newer. TypeScript projects keep their existing TypeScript ESLint
parser configuration.

To share a checkout or prerelease without a registry, produce a portable archive
from this package directory:

```sh
npm pack --pack-destination /tmp
```

In the target project:

```sh
npm install --save-dev /tmp/eslint-plugin-qwik-guards-0.1.0.tgz
```

Add the preset to the project's existing flat ESLint config, after its parser
configuration. Restrict `files` to the project's Qwik source roots if it contains
other frameworks:

```js
import qwikGuards from "eslint-plugin-qwik-guards";

export default [
  // Existing ESLint, Qwik, and TypeScript configurations go here.
  {
    ...qwikGuards.configs.recommended,
    files: ["src/**/*.{jsx,tsx}"],
  },
];
```

The preset enables `qwik-guards/no-empty-array-before-sibling` and
`qwik-guards/no-plain-jsx-form-wrapper` at `warn` severity.
To block merges after existing sites have been reviewed, override the rules to
`error` in a later config entry, or use ESLint's `--max-warnings 0` policy.

content.thinking:
I've got enough of the codebase now to start on the foundation, so I'll settle the design first. I'm going with "The Living Press": Twyne is a print shop and writers' room, and the motion comes from printing and editorial work. Fresh text reads as wet ink, slightly glossier and darker, and it dries once it's saved to disk, which signals that it's persisted locally. Committing actions should feel like a press impression.

I'm working through the rest of the visual vocabulary now: paper grain and a desk lamp for the sheet, a cobalt ink for outgoing posts to the AI providers, vermilion for corrections and published work, and non-photo blue for selection marks that don't reproduce in print.

I'm mapping each consequence class to its own motion and color: local changes stay graphite and quiet, synced ones get a settling carbon-copy shadow, provider calls are cobalt and slide out like airmail, public publishing is a vermilion press impression, and destructive actions need a hold with a hatched red cut line. Each interactive element will carry a data-consequence attribute that the foundation CSS reads, and a small DestinationTag will show where the action goes and what it costs.

I'm now working out the hold-to-confirm pattern for destructive actions: a pointer hold of roughly 600–900ms fills an ink bar, and keyboard users get a two-step arm-then-confirm instead, with releasing early cancelling. I'm also weighing whether the scaleX fill counts as motion for reduced-motion users, since colour and opacity changes are generally exempt under WCAG 2.3.3.

I'm settling the motion preferences next: `full` is the default for users with no reduced-motion preference, and I'm weighing how `calm` should differ from it. For the hold-to-confirm, I'm thinking the `still` mode should swap the timed hold for a plain two-step arm-then-confirm click, since that removes both the time pressure and the motion.

I'm laying out the motion modes now: full keeps everything including ambient life, calm drops the idle and lamp effects and shortens durations, and still removes all movement and keeps only colour and opacity changes. The preference will be saved locally and applied to the page before first paint, with the system setting deciding between full and still by default, and the durations will scale from a single motion token.

I'm looking at how the global reduced-motion rule should override the existing media-query blocks, since the new `still` preference won't trigger those. I'm planning a `data-motion="still"` selector that collapses animation and transition durations to near zero.

I'm checking how the global reduced-motion reset should interact with the OS setting, since the existing media-query blocks won't fire when someone picks "still" manually. I'm also thinking about a shared motion helper that combines the saved preference with the system setting, so the JavaScript animations and the CSS can agree.

I'm weighing whether an explicit "Full" setting should be able to override an OS-level reduce preference, given that the legacy CSS will still honour that query. I'm leaning toward keeping the choices simple as System, Full, Calm and Still, with the new CSS keyed only off the `data-motion` attribute and the bootstrap resolving System to either full or still.

I'm laying out the frequency budget next: per-keystroke work gets no layout or transform motion at all, just paint-level highlighting that stays constant regardless of document size. Caret moves and hovers stay under about 120ms and use only opacity, colour, or transform, while panels and saves get 160–320ms, and rare moments like publishing can run up to 900ms but are always skippable.

Writing CSS design tokens...

I'm working out the easing curves now: a house curve for most motion, a steeper one for exits, a press curve, and a light spring with a small overshoot for slide-ins, plus a heavier platen curve for stamps.

Writing a spring easing curve with a small overshoot for the slide-ins...

Working out the spring curve for the slide-ins: I'll compute a damped spring with a damping ratio around 0.7, which gives a small overshoot of roughly 4–5%, and sample it into a `linear()` easing list. Running a quick script to generate the points.

Still writing the consequence color tokens...

I'm weighing whether public publishing should share the vermilion red already used for the accent. Two reds could blur together, so I'm leaning toward distinguishing destructive actions with a hatched treatment and glyphs rather than colour alone.

I'm weighing whether destructive actions should be marked by a hatched pattern rather than a colour, since vermilion and the red I'd use for destructive actions are too close to tell apart. I'd rather the cut line carry the meaning through its shape than through hue alone.

I'm picking glyphs for each consequence level so the states read without relying on colour alone. A pencil for local work and a carbon-copy symbol for synced seem to fit the print-shop theme, and I'm weighing whether the pencil clashes with the one already used for empty comments.

I'm checking whether the existing Icon component already has the glyphs I need before drawing new ones. If it doesn't, I'll write small inline SVGs for each consequence level, using a pencil, two sheets, an envelope with an arrow, a stamp, and a dele mark, all at 12px with currentColor strokes.

I'm planning a ProseMirror plugin, a TipTap extension called WetInk, that tracks which ranges have been typed since the last save. Instead of decorations, which would re-render the DOM on every keystroke, I'm weighing the CSS Custom Highlight API, since computing those DOM ranges from document positions could be costly on each change.

I'm settling on a highlight approach for wet ink: the freshly typed text gets a faint glossy sheen, using a slightly darker tone and a soft shadow to suggest ink that hasn't dried yet.

I'm checking whether Chrome actually applies text-shadow to ::highlight, since that decides whether the wet-ink bleed can work through the Custom Highlight API. The plan is to test it in headless Chromium before committing to that approach.

I'm working out the wet-ink effect with the Custom Highlight API: it would move through three stages, wet, tacky, then dry, stepping about every 250ms after save. The `twyne:draft-saved` event from the IDB commit would be the trigger, so the ink dries roughly 1–1.5 seconds after typing stops, once the text is actually persisted.

I'm checking whether wet ink should still show in "still" mode, since it's a colour change rather than motion. I'm leaning toward keeping it, while still offering a setting to turn it off, and I'll update the ranges on compositionend rather than during IME composition.

I'm still weighing whether wet ink should stay on in the calmer modes, and I'm leaning toward keeping it everywhere since it reports real save state, just subtly. In zen mode I'll keep it too, because it's a property of the text itself rather than chrome. If a save fails, the ink simply stays wet, which is an honest signal that the text isn't persisted yet. When the folio changes I'll clear the ranges, and I'll make sure remote collaborative edits from the sync layer don't count as the user's fresh ink.

I'm settling the caret as vermilion, since it's high-contrast on the cream paper and works in the darker night theme too, and it stays in zen mode. I'm not animating the native caret on each keystroke; I'm considering a custom smooth caret only for jumps like clicks and navigation.

I'm picking a selection colour that echoes a blue pencil mark: non-photo blue at around 55% over the cream paper, with the ink text staying dark enough to read, and a lower alpha for the night theme so light text still holds up.

I'm naming the non-photo blue token, with a slightly deeper variant for the night theme, and noting that the current saturated system-blue selection with white text clashes with the paper. For the selection popover, I'm planning a short entry animation that slides it in from the side of the selection it's placed on, but I need to keep its transform clear of the existing placement offset.

I'm working out how the selection actions animate in: using the `translate` and `scale` properties so the entry doesn't clash with the existing placement transform. I'm also planning small destination marks on each button, cobalt for outgoing AI requests and the local/synced glyph for comments and revisions, with a tooltip saying where the passage goes.

# Instrument illustration and motion The illustrations give each instrument a recognizable purpose at a glance. They belong beside an instrument title or inside its empty state. They do not enter the manuscript, replace a button label, or imply that a provider is available. ## Direction The [original study](../public/assets/instruments/direction-study-v1.png) compares three treatments of the same composing tools: copperplate engraving, letterpress cutouts, and a paper miniature. Copperplate was selected after the parent agent's visual review because it belongs with Twyne's existing engraved editorial assets. This was an implementation choice under the art request, not an explicit user choice. Four transparent vignettes share opaque ivory paper, warm-black engraved contours, and a small vermilion mark: - **Sentence bench:** two wording slips, a composing stick, and a correction pencil. - **Threads:** two passages joined by one visible thread. - **Research:** a folder holding two marked source clippings. - **Scene:** a compact paper stage with a doorway and window. The pale paper interiors and fine edge highlights keep the silhouettes readable on Nightpress. Color is part of the artwork, not a status system. Original PNGs, exact prompts, provenance, hashes, dimensions, and export sizes are in [the asset directory](../public/assets/instruments/manifest.json). The built-in `image_gen` tool produced the artwork. WebP exports only resize and encode it; they retain the generated alpha and color. ## Components ```tsx import { InstrumentArt, InstrumentRule, } from "~/components/instruments/instrument-art"; import { InstrumentMotion, InstrumentMotionPart, } from "~/components/instruments/instrument-motion";

Sentence bench

{currentSentence} {completeAlternative} {explanation} ; ``` `kind` is `sentence-bench`, `threads`, `research`, or `scene`. The fixed sizes are 64, 128, and 192 CSS pixels for `compact`, `standard`, and `large`. Assets are 512px wide and 43–81KB apiece. Art is decorative by default with an empty alt and hidden wrapper. A `label` prop makes an illustration informative where necessary; omit it beside a heading that already explains the tool. `InstrumentTexture` is an optional, static alpha-mask texture for an illustration's own positioned container. Its ink follows the current theme at 4.5% opacity. Keep it off prose and controls. `InstrumentRule` follows the theme's ink and needs an accompanying text result; it does not announce success by itself. ## Motion contract images README.md SHA256SUMS source-assets.json source-page.md specification.md

# The living press

Twyne's interface is a working press room, not a document viewer. Most editors animate to seem modern. Here, motion has three jobs:

1. **Answer.** When a writer presses something, the room shows that it took the press.
2. **Say where things go.** Every action that sends words somewhere looks like it is sending them there, in the same ink every time.
3. **Show that the room is alive.** Editors read, ink dries and the light moves. None of it gets in the way of writing.

This page is the contract for all of it. The tokens live in [`src/styles/motion.css`](../../src/styles/motion.css), the levels and typing signal in [`src/utils/motion.ts`](../../src/utils/motion.ts), and the destinations in [`src/utils/consequence.ts`](../../src/utils/consequence.ts).

## Five rules

1. **The manuscript never moves.** Nothing translates, scales or reflows prose, and nothing lays out again because something animated. Ink may change colour on the page. Popovers, slips and margins move around the page, never on it.
2. **Frequency sets the budget.** The more often something happens, the less it may move.

   | How often | Example | Allowed |
   |---|---|---|
   | Every keystroke | typing, caret | colour only, at most one DOM write per burst, no transform |
   | Many times a minute | hover, a press | ≤ `--dur-press` / `--dur-release` (120 / 160 ms), 1px of travel |
   | A few times a minute | menus, popovers, a note arriving | ≤ `--dur-arrive` / `--dur-settle` (240 / 320 ms) |
   | A few times a session | a verdict, a publish, a first save | ≤ `--dur-ceremony` (900 ms), may use a shader |
   | Ambient | the desk lamp, an editor reading | slower than one cycle per 5 s, paused while typing |

   Keyboard-initiated actions skip their entrance where the result appears under the hands, as in command palettes and shortcuts.
3. **Consequence has one ink.** A control that sends something somewhere carries `data-consequence` and, wherever space allows, a [`<DestinationTag>`](../../src/components/ui/destination-tag.tsx). The ink is never the only cue. Every destination also has a word and a mark shape.
4. **Ambient life rests.** Anything nobody asked for carries `data-ambient` (or `.is-ambient`). It pauses while `html[data-typing]` is set, during flow and settling, and below the `full` level. Ambient work must not run per frame: it renders when its inputs change, not on a loop.
5. **Still is still.** `html[data-motion="still"]` collapses every duration. Colour and opacity changes remain, because WCAG 2.3.3 counts movement, not colour. So every state needs a colour or wording cue that does not depend on travel.

## Levels

The writer picks the level in **Preferences → Appearance → Motion**. It is stored on the device and stamped onto `<html data-motion>` before first paint.

| Level | Feedback & arrivals | Ceremonies | Ambient |
|---|---|---|---|
| `full` | yes | full length | yes, resting while typing |
| `calm` | yes | shortened (`--dur-ceremony` 360 ms) | no |
| `still` | no movement; colour only | no movement | no |

`system` (the default) resolves to `full`, or to `still` when the operating system asks for reduced motion. In script, use `allowsMotion("feedback" | "ceremony" | "ambient")` instead of reading `matchMedia` directly. Shaders must check it before allocating a context.

## Tokens

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--ease-set` | `cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1)` | the house curve; most transitions |
| `--ease-lift` | `cubic-bezier(.55,0,1,.45)` | things leaving |
| `--ease-slip` | spring `linear()`, ~3% overshoot | paper in hand: slips, notes, popovers |
| `--ease-platen` | spring `linear()`, <1% overshoot | stamps, presses, anything heavy |
| `--dur-press` / `--dur-release` | 120 / 160 ms | presses, hovers |
| `--dur-arrive` / `--dur-settle` | 240 / 320 ms | menus, slips / panels, cards |
| `--dur-ceremony` | 900 ms | verdicts, publishing |
| `--dur-dry` | 1600 ms | fresh ink drying after a save |
| `--dur-breath` | 9 s | ambient cycles |
| `--lift-1/2/3` | 1px / .25rem / .6rem | travel distances |

Shared keyframes: `press-slip-in`, `press-slip-in-from-right`, `press-fade-in`, `press-ink-flash` (tint with `--flash-ink`), and `press-impress`. Utility classes: `.press-arrive`, `.press-arrive-right`, `.press-fade`.

## Consequence grammar

| `data-consequence` | Ink | Mark | Word | Means |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `local` | ink-muted | hollow ring | device | stays on this device |
| `synced` | green | filled dot | account | copied to the writer's own account |
| `provider` | cobalt | filled dot | model | read by the writer's own model provider (BYOK) |
| `credit` | mustard | filled dot | credit | read by a hosted model; spends credit |
| `public` | vermilion | ring with dot | public | readable by anyone with the link, or a PDS |
| `erase` | deep vermilion | struck square | erases | removed and cannot be brought back here |

`aiConsequenceFor(settings)` / `loadAiConsequence()` decide between `provider` and `credit` from the writer's saved settings, so a tag tells the truth about the route a request will take.

**Guards scale with the loss.**

- Anything recoverable gets no confirmation. Undo is enough.
- A loss that is recoverable elsewhere (restore keeps a checkpoint) gets an inline confirm.
- A loss that cannot be recovered from here (erase synced history, stop sharing, unpublish) gets [`<HoldToConfirm>`](../../src/components/ui/hold-to-confirm.tsx). The platen comes down while the control is held, and releasing early drains the ink. Keyboard and assistive technology use a two-step press instead.

## The joy ledger

Each surface gets one idea that belongs to a press room and nowhere else. The table lists what it is, what it says, and why it suits that surface.

### The manuscript (lane A)

| Surface | The idea | What it communicates |
|---|---|---|
| Typing | **Wet ink.** New words are set in a slightly bluer, wetter ink until they are stored on the device, then dry to black over `--dur-dry`. Uses the CSS Custom Highlight API, so no DOM, layout or transform is touched. | Your words are safe the moment they dry. If ink stays wet, the save hasn't landed. |
| Caret | A vermilion caret, the editor's pencil. Never smoothed or animated, because Word's gliding caret is the cautionary tale. | Where the hand is. Instant. |
| Selection | Non-photo blue, the copy editor's proof pencil, instead of the system highlight. | A marked passage, ready for a decision. |
| Selection popover | Slides up off the line like a slip pushed across the desk. Every AI action carries its destination tag. | Which actions stay here and which send the passage to a model, before you press. |
| Section drag | The ⋮⋮ handle becomes a type slug that lifts on grab, and the drop is a vermilion composing rule. | Moving a section is moving set type: the whole block goes. |
| File drop | "Drop a plate" with the destination written on the docket: kept in the manuscript on this device, or uploaded to your account's storage. | Where the image will live before you let go. |
| The desk lamp | A soft light pools on the paper's grain behind the page. It drifts with the hour and leans toward the pointer only when you are not typing. | The room is lit and inhabited, and quiet while you write. |

### The editor chrome (lane B)

| Surface | The idea | What it communicates |
|---|---|---|
| Drawer | Folios slide out like a drawer of filed sheets. The active folio wears a tab, and switching moves the tab. | Which manuscript is on the desk. |
| Masthead | The wordmark's ink sits still while you type. The infinite wobble now plays only at rest, as ambient life. | A press at rest and a press at work. |
| Save and sync | One status line instead of two dots. It reads *set* on save, *on the wire* while syncing, and *filed* when the account has it. | Exactly where the latest words are. |
| Menus and popovers | One arrival everywhere: `--dur-arrive` with `--ease-slip` from the trigger side. One scrim value. | Menus belong to what opened them. |
| Publish and share | Publish is a ceremony: the button inks in vermilion as the page goes out. Unpublish and stop-sharing are held, not clicked. | Public actions look public, and permanent ones resist a slip. |
| Zen and flow | Chrome eases out as one sheet, not piece by piece, and returns the same way. | The room steps back as a whole when you write. |

### The writers' room (lane C)

| Surface | The idea | What it communicates |
|---|---|---|
| An editor reading | The portrait of an editor who is reading wears a slow pencil-mark ring, its progress tied to the real stream (reasoning → writing → filed). There is no spinner. | Who is reading your draft right now, and how far they have got. |
| A note arriving | The note is set like a slip pushed onto the board. On filing it takes a small ink impression in the editor's colour. | Something new is on the board, and from whom. |
| Asking the room | Each AI button carries its destination tag (model or credit). | Before pressing: whose model reads this, and whether it costs. |

1. **Answer.** When a writer presses something, the room shows that it took the press.
2. **Say where things go.** Every action that sends words somewhere looks like it is sending them there, in the same ink every time.
3. **Show that the room is alive.** Editors read, ink dries and the light moves. None of it gets in the way of writing.

This page is the contract for all of it. The tokens live in [`src/styles/motion.css`](../../src/styles/motion.css), the levels and typing signal in [`src/utils/motion.ts`](../../src/utils/motion.ts), and the destinations in [`src/utils/consequence.ts`](../../src/utils/consequence.ts).

## Five rules

1. **The manuscript never moves.** Nothing translates, scales or reflows prose, and nothing lays out again because something animated. Ink may change colour on the page. Popovers, slips and margins move around the page, never on it.
2. **Frequency sets the budget.** The more often something happens, the less it may move.

   | How often | Example | Allowed |
   |---|---|---|
   | Every keystroke | typing, caret | colour only, at most one DOM write per burst, no transform |
   | Many times a minute | hover, a press | ≤ `--dur-press` / `--dur-release` (120 / 160 ms), 1px of travel |
   | A few times a minute | menus, popovers, a note arriving | ≤ `--dur-arrive` / `--dur-settle` (240 / 320 ms) |
   | A few times a session | a verdict, a publish, a first save | ≤ `--dur-ceremony` (900 ms), may use a shader |
   | Ambient | the desk lamp, an editor reading | slower than one cycle per 5 s, paused while typing |

   Keyboard-initiated actions skip their entrance where the result appears under the hands, as in command palettes and shortcuts.
3. **Consequence has one ink.** A control that sends something somewhere carries `data-consequence` and, wherever space allows, a [`<DestinationTag>`](../../src/components/ui/destination-tag.tsx). The ink is never the only cue. Every destination also has a word and a mark shape.
4. **Ambient life rests.** Anything nobody asked for carries `data-ambient` (or `.is-ambient`). It pauses while `html[data-typing]` is set, during flow and settling, and below the `full` level. Ambient work must not run per frame: it renders when its inputs change, not on a loop.
5. **Still is still.** `html[data-motion="still"]` collapses every duration. Colour and opacity changes remain, because WCAG 2.3.3 counts movement, not colour. So every state needs a colour or wording cue that does not depend on travel.

## Levels

The writer picks the level in **Preferences → Appearance → Motion**. It is stored on the device and stamped onto `<html data-motion>` before first paint.

| Level | Feedback & arrivals | Ceremonies | Ambient |
|---|---|---|---|
| `full` | yes | full length | yes, resting while typing |
| `calm` | yes | shortened (`--dur-ceremony` 360 ms) | no |
| `still` | no movement; colour only | no movement | no |

`system` (the default) resolves to `full`, or to `still` when the operating system asks for reduced motion. In script, use `allowsMotion("feedback" | "ceremony" | "ambient")` instead of reading `matchMedia` directly. Shaders must check it before allocating a context.

## Tokens

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--ease-set` | `cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1)` | the house curve; most transitions |
| `--ease-lift` | `cubic-bezier(.55,0,1,.45)` | things leaving |
| `--ease-slip` | spring `linear()`, ~3% overshoot | paper in hand: slips, notes, popovers |
| `--ease-platen` | spring `linear()`, <1% overshoot | stamps, presses, anything heavy |
| `--dur-press` / `--dur-release` | 120 / 160 ms | presses, hovers |
| `--dur-arrive` / `--dur-settle` | 240 / 320 ms | menus, slips / panels, cards |
| `--dur-ceremony` | 900 ms | verdicts, publishing |
| `--dur-dry` | 1600 ms | fresh ink drying after a save |
| `--dur-breath` | 9 s | ambient cycles |
| `--lift-1/2/3` | 1px / .25rem / .6rem | travel distances |

Shared keyframes: `press-slip-in`, `press-slip-in-from-right`, `press-fade-in`, `press-ink-flash` (tint with `--flash-ink`), and `press-impress`. Utility classes: `.press-arrive`, `.press-arrive-right`, `.press-fade`.

## Consequence grammar

| `data-consequence` | Ink | Mark | Word | Means |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `local` | ink-muted | hollow ring | device | stays on this device |
| `synced` | green | filled dot | account | copied to the writer's own account |
| `provider` | cobalt | filled dot | model | read by the writer's own model provider (BYOK) |
| `credit` | mustard | filled dot | credit | read by a hosted model; spends credit |
| `public` | vermilion | ring with dot | public | readable by anyone with the link, or a PDS |
| `erase` | deep vermilion | struck square | erases | removed and cannot be brought back here |

input.command:
git add -A src/utils/motion.ts src/utils/motion.test.ts src/utils/consequence.ts src/utils/consequence.test.ts src/utils/hold-press.ts src/components/ui/destination-tag.tsx src/components/ui/hold-to-confirm.tsx src/styles docs/design/living-press.md src/global.css src/root.tsx src/routes/settings/index.tsx src/components/editor/twyne-editor.tsx && git status --short && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Lay the living press foundation: motion levels, tokens and consequence inks

One vocabulary for every animated surface, so the lanes that follow give
each part of the room its own life without each inventing timings.

- Motion levels (full, calm, still) chosen in Preferences, stamped onto
  <html data-motion> before first paint like the palette. System follows
  the OS reduced-motion switch, live.
- Tokens in src/styles/motion.css: the house curve, two spring linear()
  easings generated from a damped spring, durations by frequency, and
  registered properties for ink fills and the lamp.
- Consequence inks and <DestinationTag>: one ink, mark and word per
  destination (device, account, model, credit, public, erases).
- <HoldToConfirm> for permanent losses, with a two-step keyboard path.
- A typing signal (html[data-typing]) set once per burst, so ambient life
  rests while the writer types.
- One stylesheet per surface for the lanes, and docs/design/living-press.md
  as the contract: rules, budget, grammar and the joy ledger.
- Fixes: .dept-label no longer tightens on hover, the second .icon-btn
  definition is folded into the first, .btn-paper has a disabled state.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline -2

input.task:
You are Lane B of a four-lane effort called "the living press" in Twyne, a Qwik 2 + TipTap local-first writing app (editorial letterpress brand: paper, ink, stamps, vermilion and cobalt). Your worktree starts from commit 0fd76e12 on branch feat/living-press, which contains the shared foundation. Commit your work on your own branch; the parent merges it.

## Read first (the contract)
- docs/design/living-press.md: the five rules, the frequency budget, the consequence grammar, and your rows in "The joy ledger → The editor chrome (lane B)". Implement those rows.
- src/styles/motion.css: tokens (--ease-set, --ease-lift, --ease-slip, --ease-platen, --dur-press/release/arrive/settle/ceremony/dry/breath, --lift-1/2/3), consequence inks (--ink-local/synced/provider/credit/public/erase via [data-consequence] → var(--consequence-ink)), shared keyframes press-slip-in, press-slip-in-from-right, press-fade-in, press-ink-flash, press-impress, and classes .press-arrive/.press-arrive-right/.press-fade. Ambient motion must carry data-ambient (paused automatically while html[data-typing], in flow/settling, and below full). html[data-motion="still"] collapses durations globally.
- src/utils/motion.ts (allowsMotion, motionLevel, onMotionLevelChange, markTyping/isTyping), src/utils/consequence.ts (Consequence type, aiConsequenceFor, loadAiConsequence), src/components/ui/destination-tag.tsx (<DestinationTag to="public" />), src/components/ui/hold-to-confirm.tsx (<HoldToConfirm onConfirm$ label hint consequence="erase">…</HoldToConfirm>).

## Files you own (edit ONLY these, plus new files you create under src/components/editor/chrome/ if needed)
- src/styles/press-chrome.css (your stylesheet; already imported from global.css: put ALL your new CSS here, do not edit global.css)
- src/routes/editor/index.tsx (drawer, masthead, sign-in toast, hydration gate, board toggle, zen/flow handling)
- src/components/folio/folio-menu.tsx (File menu, import modal, share/publish modal)
- src/components/collaboration/share-dialog.tsx
- src/components/auth/account-menu.tsx
- src/components/editor/sync-indicator.tsx and sync-indicator-helpers.ts
- src/components/editor/typst-workspace.tsx (+ typst-workspace.css)
- src/components/editor/compositor-panel.tsx (only open/close of pickers/popovers and tab indicator; do not restructure)
- src/components/editor/shortcut-dialog.tsx
- src/components/brief/project-brief-card.tsx
Do NOT edit: src/global.css, src/styles/motion.css, other press-*.css files, src/components/editor/twyne-editor.tsx, manuscript-panel.tsx, selection-actions.tsx, anything under personas/rubric/comments/citations/editorial-board/living-desk/instruments/desk. Other lanes own those, and your branch must merge cleanly.

## What to build (concrete)
1. Drawer: slides like a drawer of filed sheets. The active folio wears a vermilion tab (a small ::before mark) that moves to the newly active row on switch (use a transition on a shared indicator, or animate the new row's tab in with --ease-slip; keep it cheap). Inner content fades/slides with the width change instead of being clipped. The drawer toggle icon reflects open/closed (aria-expanded + a visual state).
2. Masthead: the TWYNE wordmark's `.press` infinite wobble must become ambient: give the wordmark data-ambient so it rests while typing/in flow/below full. Do not edit global.css's .press rule; add the attribute in index.tsx.
3. Save and sync status line: replace the bare SyncDot + "Saved Xs ago" pairing in the status bar with one status line whose words say where the latest words are: "set" (stored on this device), "on the wire" (syncing), "filed" (in the account), "held on this device" (offline/local-only/error with reason). Use the consequence inks (local hollow, synced green). Animate only state changes (a brief press-ink-flash with --flash-ink on transition to filed), never a perpetual pulse. Remove the duplicate SyncDot in the compositor quick actions if it is the same indicator (sync-indicator.tsx is yours; compositor-panel.tsx usage line is yours to change).
4. Menus and popovers: give the File menu dropdown, AccountMenu dropdown, ShareDialog popover, compositor pickers, the Typst status popover and the shortcut dialog ONE consistent arrival: --dur-arrive with --ease-slip, translating --lift-2 from the trigger side, plus press-fade-in for scrims. Use one scrim colour token for all modal scrims (define it in press-chrome.css, e.g. --scrim: color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-ink) 55%, transparent)). Prefer CSS-only (@starting-style or keyframes on mount). Nothing may delay interactivity.
5. Publish and share (folio-menu.tsx and share-dialog.tsx): add <DestinationTag> to: Publish now (public), PDS publish (public), Micropub (public), Invite (synced, or public if it shares beyond the account; read the code), Share this folio (synced), exports (local). Publish success becomes a short ceremony: the button inks vermilion across (use --press-progress or a keyframe with --dur-ceremony and --ease-platen) and settles to a "published" state. Unpublish, Unpublish from PDS, remove collaborator and Stop sharing use <HoldToConfirm consequence="erase"> (or "public" for unpublish if you judge the loss as un-publishing; state your reasoning in the report). Stop sharing currently opens a ThemedDialog; replacing the dialog with a hold is fine if focus/keyboard behaviour is preserved.
6. Hydration gate ("Press Room / Setting the type…" around index.tsx line 1110): keep it but make it calm and on-brand: a press-fade with a 150ms delay so fast loads never flash it, and a quiet set-type line (e.g. a row of slugs filling) marked data-ambient. Do NOT restructure hydration; a separate effort will remove the gate.
7. Sign-in toast: arrive with press-slip-in from below, use the shared --shade-based shadow instead of the hard-coded rgba, radius 2px like the rest.
8. Zen and flow: when zen toggles, chrome eases out/in as one sheet: a single opacity+translate transition on the masthead and compositor using --dur-settle and --ease-set. Fix the dead `.zen-masthead` hover strip: either make it work (a thin hover strip that reveals the masthead) or remove the class usage from index.tsx; explain the choice.
9. Disabled states: undo/redo in compositor use opacity .4 like .btn-press (they use .3 today); .typst-apply needs a visible disabled style (typst-workspace.css).

## Rules
- The manuscript never moves. Nothing you add may shift prose layout.
- Durations and easing come only from the tokens. No new hard-coded cubic-beziers, no transition: all.
- Every state you animate also has a colour or wording cue (for still mode).
- Keep accessibility: aria-expanded/aria-pressed correct, focus returned on close, keyboard paths intact, HoldToConfirm keyboard flow works.
- Match the surrounding code's comment density and idiom (Qwik component$, useSignal, class arrays). Don't add stock caveat copy.
- Performance: no per-frame JS, no listeners on keystrokes.

## Verify before you finish
- `bun install` if node_modules is missing; `bun run prompts:compile && bun run i18n:prepare` once.
- `npx eslint <your changed files>` clean (warnings only if pre-existing).
- Targeted typecheck: write a temp tsconfig that extends ./tsconfig.json with include = your changed files + src/qwik-v2-compat.d.ts, src/popmelt.d.ts, qwik.env.d.ts, src/types/wav-encoder.d.ts, and run `npx tsc -p <it> --noEmit`. Do NOT run full `bun run test` or full-project tsc.
- Run any existing tests next to the files you touched (e.g. `bun test src/components/editor/sync-indicator*.test.ts` if present, `bun test tests/<relevant>`).
- Optional visual check: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5191 bun run dev.frontend` and a headless Playwright script run with `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH node script.mjs` (seed IndexedDB via `await import("/src/utils/idb.ts")` in page context as e2e/instruments.e2e.ts does; route /api/auth/ to null). Save screenshots under artifacts/qa-recordings/2026-11-05/juice/lane-b/.
- Commit with a clear message ending with a blank line and `Co-Authored-By: GPT-6.1 Terra <noreply@openai.com>`.

## Report back
Branch name and head SHA; a table of each ledger row → what you built → file:line; any row you skipped and why; verification commands and their results; anything another lane must know (e.g. a token you wished existed).

input.task:
You are Lane C of a four-lane effort called "the living press" in Twyne, a Qwik 2 + TipTap local-first writing app with an AI "room of editors" (personas) that leave notes, a rubric that stamps a grade, research ("Apparatus") and instruments. Commit your work on your own branch; the parent merges it.
