This is the supported T3 transport fallback, not an ordinary shell-based substitute for delegation.

### Showing visuals

When a chart, table, diagram, image collage, or mockup would say more than prose, build a self-contained HTML page, check it with `html_preview`, then publish it with `html_render` before your final reply. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

- When model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty `inheritedOptions` from `orchestrator_capabilities`, use `delegate_task` even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Read the selected model's descriptors from `orchestrator_capabilities` and put settings in `target.options`, not only in the prompt. Claude commonly uses {"effort":"max","fastMode":true}; Codex uses {"reasoningEffort":"max","serviceTier":"priority"}. Do not translate max to high or ignore unsupported settings: report a capability mismatch. Options inherit only for the same provider instance and model; explicit entries override individual values, and [] or {} clears them. Check the returned providerInstanceId, model, and options against the requested selection.


### Background work you wait on

Before you end your turn to wait for a background command or Monitor you started, such as tests, a build, or a CI wait, call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID. The thread then stays in the user's Working list until that task ends, instead of returning to them early. Do not mark a dev server, a watcher, or anything else you leave running.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

args.description: Optional arguments for the skill

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__delegate_task
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Delegate one task to a T3-owned child agent/subagent of THIS thread and run it with only the supplied task prompt, without copying parent conversation history. Choose providers and models from orchestrator_capabilities, which uses the same live catalog as the composer. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use this for any model missing from the native tool, including same-provider work, for cross-provider work, or for explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call delegate_task again with the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in the task prompt. Track each round by its own taskId and use a distinct clientRequestId per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use t3_thread_send on its childThreadId. Set isolation to worktree for a separate checkout based on the parent local commit, with project setup completed before the child starts. Uncommitted edits are not copied; omitted isolation shares the parent checkout. Use delegate_task when model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty inheritedOptions from orchestrator_capabilities, even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Set target.options using advertised IDs: Claude {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Check providerInstanceId, model, and options in the result. Provider/model and modes inherit unless overridden. Options inherit only for the same instance and model; explicit entries override individual values and [] or {} clears them. A requested runtimeMode must be one the target provider lists in orchestrator_capabilities runtimeModes; an inherited one steps down to the broadest mode it offers. Leave runtimeMode unset unless the user asks for a supervised child: approval-required and auto-accept-edits usually make the child wait for a person at each action that needs approval. Prefer mode='async' for long work; mode='wait' blocks until completion, a blocking question, a pending approval, or timeout. If hasPendingQuestion, pass threadId=childThreadId to t3_pending_request_list, t3_pending_request_read (with requestId) and t3_pending_request_respond, or ask the user; the task's completion still wakes this thread. If pendingApproval is set, read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback. It grants no approval authority; decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder, and pending request tools answer questions only. The child keeps running and its completion still wakes this thread. timeoutMs on mode=wait is only the parent's wait budget and does not cancel the child. waitTimedOut on that wait call means the timeout fired; keep that taskId and read status on later task_status. An async child's completion wakes this thread through a notification, steered into active turns where supported or queued otherwise, so end the turn instead of polling or spawning watchers; use task_status only when the result is needed mid-turn.

anyOf.description: Model options from orchestrator_capabilities. For the same provider instance and model, overrides individual inherited values; [] or {} clears them. Claude: {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex: {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Only use options advertised by the selected model.
Defaults to shared: use the parent's checkout. Worktree creates a separate checkout from the parent's current local commit before starting the child. Uncommitted edits are not copied.

Defaults to async. Use wait only when this turn needs the child's result before you can continue. A blocking question or a pending approval in the child ends the wait early with the task still running.

timeoutMs.description: Wait budget for mode=wait only. Default 10 minutes. Elapsing it returns waitTimedOut=true on that call and does not cancel the child.

anyOf.description: Defaults to inherit; omit it unless the user asks for a supervised child. A narrower mode is not a read-only switch: on most providers, approval-required and auto-accept-edits pause the child at each action that needs approval until a person approves it in the child's thread, which this thread cannot do. To limit what the child does, say so in the task. A mode ranked above this thread's is rejected; that ranking does not promise the child's provider permissions are narrower than this thread's.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_preview
tools.description: Render an HTML page in T3's headless browser and get back a PNG screenshot, contentHeight (the height the page needs at this width), and its console output: log, info, warning, error, and uncaught exceptions, with stack traces pointing into page.html. console.log is a fine way to report your own checks. Use it to check and iterate on a page before html_render. The first preview on a machine can report that T3 is still installing its preview browser; call again a minute later. Write one self-contained document with inline <style> and <script>. Local images written as absolute file paths (src="/abs/shot.png", CSS url(/abs/bg.webp), or a JS string) are inlined automatically; remote http(s) URLs, such as a CDN chart library, load as-is. The page gets the theme variables and layout described in html_render.

anyOf.description: Viewport width in CSS pixels, 240-1600. Defaults to 728, the reply column; use about 390 to check phones.
Theme to preview. Defaults to dark.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_render
tools.description: Show a finished HTML page (chart, table, diagram, collage, mockup) inline in this thread, above your final text reply; call it before writing that reply. The reader already sees the page, so the reply should not announce it, say where it is, or restate it: add only what the page doesn't say. Preview with html_preview first. T3 fits the frame to the page's height at each reader's width. On mobile, a height below the page's contentHeight caps the frame there, and the rest scrolls inside it; web and desktop fit the whole page, up to 20000px. Write one self-contained document with inline <style> and <script>. Local images written as absolute file paths (src="/abs/shot.png", CSS url(/abs/bg.webp), or a JS string) are inlined automatically; remote http(s) URLs, such as a CDN chart library, load as-is. The frame is borderless on the thread's background, as wide as the reply column (728px on desktop by default, wider if the reader widens chat, about 360px on phones), and its left edge lines up with your reply text. The page sits on the thread's own background, so by default leave html, body, and the outermost element with no background color. This overrides general style preferences such as a fixed black page background. Use a fluid width with no horizontal padding on the outermost element, and no outer card, border, or banner title: the page is part of your reply. If a box needs its own background (a mock of a specific screen, a panel that must stand apart), give it at least 16px of padding on every side and var(--radius) corners, so content never touches its edge. Give charts fixed pixel heights rather than heights that scale with width. Let content set the page's height. The frame grows to fit the page, so a height that follows the viewport makes it grow again and again: html_preview and html_render reject vh, svh, lvh, and dvh units, and height:100% on html or body has the same problem. T3 injects its active theme as CSS custom properties on :root, and they follow the user's theme and light/dark mode live: --background (page background, identical to the thread around the frame), --foreground, --muted, --muted-foreground, --card, --card-foreground, --popover, --popover-foreground, --secondary, --secondary-foreground, --border, --input, --ring, --primary, --primary-foreground (solid buttons), --accent, --accent-foreground (brand accent), --accent-surface, --accent-surface-foreground, --destructive, --destructive-foreground, --destructive-surface, --warning, --warning-foreground, --warning-surface, --success, --success-foreground, --info, --info-foreground, --code-background, --code-foreground, --chart-1 ... --chart-6 (categorical series for charts), --radius, --font-sans, --font-mono. The base stylesheet sets html background/color/font from these, body margin to 0, and hides the page's scrollbar; your own CSS overrides it.

title.description: Short name for the page.

height.description: The frame height in CSS pixels, 80-2000. Use html_preview's contentHeight. A lower height makes long content scroll inside the frame on mobile only.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__orchestrator_capabilities
tools.description: List the V2 provider instances, a short list of their models from the same live catalog as the composer, inherited runtime settings, and app-owned orchestration features available to this caller. The list has the user's favorite and custom models, your own model, every current Codex, Claude, Muse and Grok model, and the first 8 current models of other providers. Other legacy models are left out. omittedModels counts models left out; pass search, such as 'sonnet 4.6', to find them. delegate_task accepts any catalog model, listed or not. For a separate top-level thread in a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__request_secret
tools.description: Ask the user for a secret (a token, API key, signing secret, password) through a private card in this thread, and wait for them to answer. The value is kept by the app and NEVER returned to you or shown in the transcript. When saved, the result carries a secretRef: pass it to a tool that accepts one (e.g. schedule_task's signature.secretRef). It works once. Never ask for secrets in chat, and never invent one.

placeholder.description: Hint inside the input, e.g. 'Paste your GitHub token'.

timeoutMs.description: How long to wait for the user. Default 10 minutes.

clientRequestId.description: Reuse when retrying a call that lost its result, so the user sees one card and its answer is returned again. Use a new id to ask again after timed_out or cancelled.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_background_wait
tools.description: Keep this thread in the user's Working list and out of their inbox while you wait for background work. Start a background command or Monitor first. Call this before you end your turn if you will act on its result when it wakes you. In taskIds, give the ID shown when the task started. The thread stays in Working until the task ends. The user is not told the work is done. Do not mark work you leave running, such as a dev server or watcher. Unmarked commands and monitors never keep the thread in Working. Pass waiting=false to remove the mark. This does not stop the task. IDs that are not running return in unmatched and change nothing. Only Claude threads support this tool. Other providers return an error.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_read
tools.description: Read durable state and a paginated timeline from any T3 thread in this environment. The default messages view returns user messages, assistant messages, and proposed plans; activity returns all summarized timeline items. Reading an untruncated terminal assistant result from this parent thread's direct app-owned child acknowledges that child's automatic completion delivery. Continue with afterPosition=nextPosition. Recover long item text with itemId and textOffset=nextTextOffset until nextTextOffset is null; offsets count UTF-16 code units. The thread also reports its snooze state and, in pullRequests, every linked pull request; linkedPullRequest is a legacy single link and can be null while pullRequests still has entries. To link a thread for the user, write `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with the threadId exactly as returned, not URL-encoded; T3 Code shows the thread's current title.

limit.description: Maximum timeline items to return, from 1 to 100.

runLimit.description: Maximum recent runs to return, from 1 to 50.

maxCharsPerItem.description: Maximum text characters per item, from 1 to 50000.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_send
tools.description: Send a message to any T3 thread in this environment. The target cannot have broader permission modes than the caller. Use delegate_task with the full review context and a new clientRequestId for independent review rounds. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, send to its childThreadId. After the original task completes, a requested follow-up creates a fresh task in that child thread and returns taskId when it starts a turn or restarts a turn without its own task; its completion notifies the parent, and the original result stays unchanged. A steer that joins a running turn returns that turn's task, if it has one. mode='auto' starts an idle thread, steers a fully active turn, or queues behind a turn that is not yet steerable. Use queue for a separate follow-up turn, steer for an in-flight update, or restart to interrupt-and-restart the active turn. clientRequestId makes retries idempotent.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_worktree_handoff
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Move this agent thread into a new git worktree. To launch a separate agent already bound to a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy instead. Creates the worktree branch (optionally from the base branch's remote), re-points the thread at the worktree, and by default runs the project's setup script there. Changing the workspace detaches the live provider session, so the current turn ends shortly after the handoff is recorded; call this as the last action of the turn. To keep working after the handoff, pass continuationPrompt with the remaining work: it is queued as the thread's next message and starts a new turn inside the worktree with the conversation preserved. Without it the thread stays idle until the next message. The worktree is not removed automatically when the thread is deleted. Fails if the thread is already attached to a worktree.

anyOf.description: Fetch the remote baseRef belongs to and start the worktree branch from its remote-tracking commit instead of the local ref. Defaults to the server's 'new worktrees start from remote' setting.
Run the project's configured setup script in the new worktree after handoff. Defaults to true.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_worktree_list
tools.description: List branch refs and their associated checkout paths for a thread's workspace (omit threadId for this thread) using the app's ref inventory. Detached worktrees without a branch are not included. Use t3_worktree_status for the thread binding and t3_worktree_handoff to create a new worktree.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__task_status
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Read a T3-owned delegated task created by this parent thread. childRunId identifies the original delegated run. workState distinguishes working, waiting_for_children, and result_available; a completed turn with live nested work is not a completed task. summary is the final task result, including provider errors on failure, and remains stable after publication. hasPendingChildRuns reports later queued or executing turns in the backing child thread, even after the task is terminal; it does not reopen the task, and task_cancel stops those turns too. Turns held in a stopped queue wait for the user and do not count. latestTerminal* provides later non-monitor turn results; latestTerminalSummary and latestTerminalResultContextTransferId are independently null when they exactly repeat summary and resultContextTransferId, respectively. pendingApproval identifies the oldest pending live approval for this task's own unfinished work. Read the fresh full request in childThreadId before responding: the record can outlive its provider callback and grants no approval authority. Decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder. Reading a terminal result acknowledges its automatic parent delivery.

description: User wants heavy parallel Terra swarms and is fine with E2B/Railway/Cloudflare sandboxes for compute; local disk/RAM is not a reason to serialize

The user wants me to use Terra subagent swarms "as much as you can". They are fine with offloading compute to remote sandboxes, not just this machine: "u can work with e2b and railway and cloudflare sandboxes dude" (2026-10-28).

**Why:** this machine has about 55 GB free disk and 31 GB RAM, and each `desktop/gpui` ui-tests build takes about 12 GB. When I limited lane count to fit the local machine, the user pushed back.

**How to apply:**
- Fan work out to many parallel `delegate_task` lanes ([[model-nicknames-for-delegation]]).
- Put heavy builds and captures on remote sandboxes.
- Credentials (never print them):
  - E2B: `e2b_api_key@secrets` (retired for builds; see below).
  - Cloudflare: `cloudflare@secrets` plus `cloudflare_account_id@default`.
  - Railway: the CLI is already logged in.
- **Railway is the preferred remote runner** (user, 2026-10-28: "use railway instead"). The native port's runner is `desktop/gpui/tools/remote/railway.ts` (`bun run desktop.gpui.job …`). It uses project `twyne-gpui-builds` (e4ceb8e6…) with checkpoints `twyne-gpui-base` (toolchain) and `twyne-gpui-warm` (built tree). Railway sandboxes are 8 vCPU / 7 GB / 29 GB. `exec` runs without `$USER`, so set `USER=root` before sourcing `nix.sh`. Scope flags must come before `--`. The E2B runner is retired.
- Still shut down sandboxes when done, and report spend.
---
name: twyne-browser-verification
description: "How to check twyne editor UI in a real browser here — headless Playwright env fix, free port, IndexedDB folio seeding, known flaky test pair"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 2a13dcae-f7b6-4086-b45c-4b7202355290
  modified: 2026-11-04T23:31:52.214Z
---

Recipe that worked on 2026-10-17 for verifying editor UI changes without the Convex backend:

- **Port:** 5173 may belong to another project (interleave-app). Start twyne with `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 bun run dev.frontend`.
- **Headless Playwright:** importing `node_modules/playwright/index.mjs` from a scratch script works, but Chromium fails to launch (GLIBC error from a nix alsa-lib) unless run as `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH node script.mjs`.
- **Skip onboarding:** a fresh profile redirects /editor/ to /dossier/create/. Instead, seed like `e2e/instruments.e2e.ts` `seed()`: route `/api/auth/` to `null`, visit a routed blank page, `import("/src/utils/idb.ts")` in page context, then call saveFoliosToIdb / saveFolioContentToIdb / saveActiveFolioIdToIdb (+ `signin-toast-dismissed` meta, `twyne:editor:view:v1` with zenMode false).
- **T3 preview tool:** its viewport can be zoomed or scaled (innerWidth ≠ the requested size), and evaluate/snapshot time out on heavy pages. Prefer the headless script for measurements.
- **Known flaky pair (pre-existing at HEAD bfa07af1):** `struggle-tracker.test.ts` and `quick-review.test.ts` fail together in one bun run (shared System One budget state). Each passes alone. Don't blame new changes for it.
- **Running e2e:** with the dev server on 5174, `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 npx playwright test <file>` works.
  - Screenshot suites (instruments, instrument-dock, instrument-room, living-desk) must run under `--config playwright.visual.config.ts`. It starts its own server on 5187 and compares against the committed `e2e/visual-baselines/`. The default config writes stray `e2e/*-snapshots/` folders; delete them afterwards.
  - About 38 default-config e2e tests already failed at HEAD bfa07af1 (checked on 2026-10-17 against a clean worktree). The causes:
    - The Pagination extension was unregistered in 0cb77885, so `__twynePagination` never appears. This breaks all of pagination and formatting, and most of drag-selection.
    - The "Go to page" combobox needs the Typst proof, which never typesets here. This breaks editor-declutter.
    - Tests expect a visible `.twyne-toolbar`, Bold, or read-aloud control, but zen is now the default and those sit in the collapsed Compositor. This breaks __responsive, select-all and read-aloud.
    - Tests expect a "File ▾" button and other masthead and drawer flows that have since changed. This breaks import and dossier-persistence.
  - Before blaming a change, run the same files against `git worktree add --detach /tmp/twyne-base HEAD` on port 5175 and diff the failing test names. The BYOK and drop-caret tests flake.
- **WebGPU on the real Iris Xe (checked 2026-11-04):** launch Chromium with `--enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features=Vulkan --use-angle=vulkan`. The adapter then reports `intel gen-12lp` and timestamp queries work. With only `--enable-unsafe-webgpu` you get SwiftShader, a software fallback. `navigator.gpu` only exists on a secure origin: use localhost, not `about:blank`.
- **Opening a suggestion card:** click the `.twyne-mark-anchor[data-anchor-id=…]` chip. Clicking the marked words doesn't open it. The card's accept button is `button[title="Accept & stamp"]`.
- **Qwik gotcha:** a component inside a closed `<details>` never runs its `useVisibleTask$` (it has no box). Mount it only while the disclosure is open.

Related: [[skip-long-verification]]

input.task:
You are working on Twyne, a local-first writing app (Qwik 2 + TipTap/ProseMirror + Convex). Your goal is to find and fix a bug the user reported in their own words:

> "there is this scrolling bug where we see a ton of flickering as well when model is going on and just get a lot warnings that something is wrong"

## First steps
- Your worktree starts from an older local commit. Begin with `git fetch origin && git switch -c fix/flicker-during-model-runs origin/main`. `main` is v0.27.1. Run `bun install` if the lockfile changed.
- Read `CLAUDE.md`. If you touch `convex/`, also read `convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md`.
- Read these notes in `/home/diogenes/.claude/projects/-home-diogenes-Projects-apps-twyne/memory/`:
  - `twyne-browser-verification.md`: the headless Playwright recipe and IndexedDB seeding.
  - `skip-long-verification.md`
  - `dev-machine-is-old.md`
  - `no-reflexive-hedging.md`
- Run the dev server on **port 5181**: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5181 bun run dev.frontend`. Other lanes are using 5182–5185.
- Earlier perf harness scripts are in `/home/diogenes/.t3/worktrees/twyne/perf-harness/` (`idle-tab.mjs`, `multi-tab.mjs`, `typing-burst.mjs`, `perf-metric.mjs`). Run them from a Twyne checkout as `PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_VALIDATE_HOST_REQUIREMENTS=1 env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH node <script>`. Reuse or extend them.

## What to investigate
"When model is going on" is ambiguous. Cover every kind of model work the editor runs while the writer scrolls:
- writers'-room and editorial-board runs, and in-flow margin cards arriving or updating (`src/components/in-flow/flow-surface.tsx`, `src/components/editor/extensions/flow-conductor.ts`);
- live review (`src/components/writing-tools/live-review-status.tsx`, `src/utils/live-review.ts`);
- the research loop;
- grammar (Harper wasm, `src/utils/grammar.ts`);
- on-device WebGPU models. Use the Iris Xe Chromium flags from the browser note.

To make model runs happen without production accounts or spend, start a small local mock OpenAI-compatible server that streams slow tokens. Configure it as the writer's own provider (bring-your-own key in Settings, or seed the settings in IndexedDB).

Then scroll the manuscript during those runs, in both Firefox and Chromium. Capture the flicker with evidence, for example:
- layout-shift entries;
- repeated mounts of margin cards (MutationObserver);
- decoration or highlight rebuilds (wet ink uses the CSS Custom Highlight API);
- scroll-anchoring fights (`overflow-anchor`) or programmatic scrollIntoView/scrollTop writes;
- the desk lamp and running foot (`src/styles/motion.css`, `--lamp-x`/`--lamp-y`);
- long frames.

The second half of the report is "a lot warnings that something is wrong". Find exactly which warnings show during runs: UI notices (`ApplicationNotice`, live-review notices, toasts) and console errors. Find why they fire and fix the causes. Where a notice is legitimate, make it show once, not repeatedly.

## Fixes and measurement
- Fix root causes. Don't hide symptoms with blanket `animation: none` or by dropping features.
- Measure the same scenario before and after, for example per 10 s of scrolling during a run:
  - layout shifts;
  - card remounts;
  - frames over 50 ms;
  - notices shown;
  - console errors.
- Add targeted tests where logic changed.
- Run only targeted `bun test <files>`, eslint on the files you touched, and one `bun run build` at the end. Don't run the full suite or repeated full `tsc`.

## Limits
- Commit on your branch locally.
- Do not push, deploy or open PRs.
- Do not sign in or create accounts against production, and do not trigger paid or hosted AI.
- Do not change Railway variables or Convex env.
- Do not touch `/home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne`. It has the user's uncommitted work.
- Stop any servers you start, by the PID listening on your port. Never use `pkill -f`.

## Report back
- Branch and head SHA.
- What you reproduced, with numbers.
- Each cause you found and its fix, as file:line.
- Before/after measurements.
- Exactly how you verified, with commands and results.
- Anything you could not reproduce or left open.

input.title: Hover cards that stay and can be used
input.task:
You are working on Twyne, a local-first writing app (Qwik 2 + TipTap/ProseMirror + Convex). Your goal is to make the editor's hover cards stay and be usable. Here is the request in the user's own words:

> "the users when they see the hover effect they want to be able to interact with the editor that pops up and we should have a effect where the hover card that appears sticks around while the user has seen it for a time so that the user can go click on it send a reply get the non truncated view."

## First steps
- Your worktree starts from an older local commit. Begin with `git fetch origin && git switch -c feat/hover-cards-stay origin/main`. `main` is v0.27.1. Run `bun install` if the lockfile changed.
- Read `CLAUDE.md`.
- Read these notes in `/home/diogenes/.claude/projects/-home-diogenes-Projects-apps-twyne/memory/`:
  - `twyne-browser-verification.md`: the headless Playwright recipe, IndexedDB seeding, and how to open suggestion cards.
  - `skip-long-verification.md`
  - `autonomy-by-default.md`
  - `no-reflexive-hedging.md`
- Run the dev server on **port 5182**: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5182 bun run dev.frontend`.

## Where the hover paths are
There are two, and both need the fix.

1. **The floating card when the margin is not carrying notes.** In `src/components/editor/twyne-editor.tsx`, around the comment "Hover: preview a persona note below its sentence" (about line 1980):
   - `mouseover`/`mouseout` on `.twyne-persona-note`, `.twyne-comment-mark` and `.twyne-mark-anchor` drive it;
   - the state lives in `store.notePopover` / `store.userCommentPopover`, with `buildAndPin` and `OPEN_WRITER_COMMENT_EVENT`;
   - there is a 350 ms intent delay;
   - today it closes on mouseout unless `relatedTarget` is already the card. Crossing the gap between the passage and the card closes it.
2. **The margin.** `src/components/in-flow/flow-surface.tsx` uses `hoverId`/`peekId`/`lingerId`/`openId` and `hover()`. Pointing at a passage peeks its card there and draws a connection.

## What to build
A hover card the writer has actually looked at should stay.
- **Dwell.** After the card has been visible for a short dwell (pick it; roughly 600–900 ms), it becomes held. A quick pass-through never holds anything.
- **Crossing the gap.** Add a grace period and treat the pointer heading toward the card (a safe triangle) as staying. Moving from the passage to the card never closes it.
- **While held, the card is fully interactive:**
  - click into it;
  - write and send a reply in its thread;
  - expand it to the untruncated text;
  - use its existing actions.
- **It goes away** on Escape, a click elsewhere, typing in the manuscript, or a deliberate hover on another passage after a grace period.
- **Focus.** It must never steal the caret or focus while the writer is typing. v0.27.1 fixed a focus steal (`src/components/collaboration/share-dialog-focus.test.ts`); don't regress that kind of behaviour.
- **Show the held state.** Use the living-press motion system in `src/styles/motion.css`: tokens like `--dur-settle` and `--ease-set`, and keyframes like `press-impress`. For example, the card settles and pins with a subtle impression. Respect the `html[data-motion]` levels full, calm and still.
- **Zen mode** keeps its current rule: hover previews are suppressed.

## Tests and verification
- Put the hover state machine (intent, dwell, grace, held, dismiss) in a small pure module with unit tests.
- In the browser, use Playwright to:
  - move the mouse from a marked passage to its card across the gap, slowly and with a realistic path;
  - check it stays held;
  - type a reply and send it;
  - expand the full text;
  - check Escape and typing dismiss it, and a quick pass-through does not hold it.
- Check both the floating path (margin hidden) and the margin path.
- Seed a folio with persona notes or comments in IndexedDB. Look at how existing e2e tests seed them (`e2e/`).
- Run only targeted `bun test`, eslint on the files you touched, and one `bun run build` at the end. Don't run the full suite.

## Limits
- Commit on your branch locally.
- Do not push, deploy or open PRs.
- Do not sign in or create accounts against production, and do not trigger paid or hosted AI.
- Do not change Railway variables or Convex env.
- Do not touch `/home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne`.
- Stop your server by the PID on your port. Never use `pkill -f`.

## Report back
- Branch and head SHA.
- What changed and why, as file:line.
- The timings you chose.
- How you verified, with commands and results.
- Any open questions.

input.task:
You are working on Twyne, a local-first writing app (Qwik 2 + TipTap/ProseMirror + Convex). The writer wants an editor that finds the sentences that need work and offers rewrites. Here is the request in the user's own words:

> "we need another editor and loop like sentence bench that looks at sentences that are worded weirdly grammatically or otherwise that need work that give the person a bunch of rewritten options this is kind of what sentence bench was doing."

## First steps
- Your worktree starts from an older local commit. Begin with `git fetch origin && git switch -c feat/line-editor-loop origin/main`. `main` is v0.27.1. Run `bun install` if the lockfile changed.
- Read `CLAUDE.md`. If you touch `convex/`, also read `convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md` first.
- Read these notes in `/home/diogenes/.claude/projects/-home-diogenes-Projects-apps-twyne/memory/`:
  - `autonomy-by-default.md`: features run on their own, and buttons are optional overrides.
  - `no-reflexive-hedging.md`
  - `skip-long-verification.md`
  - `twyne-browser-verification.md`
  - `dev-machine-is-old.md`
  - `manual-voice-and-screenshots.md`
- Run the dev server on **port 5183**: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5183 bun run dev.frontend`.

## What exists today
- **Sentence Bench** opens for a sentence the writer is visibly struggling with, offering a trial revision and a "revision reading":
  - `src/components/in-flow/sentence-bench.tsx` and `.css`;
  - `src/utils/sentence-bench.ts`;
  - `src/components/editor/extensions/struggle-tracker.ts`;
  - `src/utils/sentence-ledger.ts`.
- **Harper** catches grammar locally: `src/utils/grammar.ts`, wasm, slim flavour.
- **Proposed edits** with word diffs and accept already exist in `src/components/editor/suggestion-panel.tsx`.
- **The instruments and the in-flow margin:**
  - `src/utils/instrument-room.ts`;
  - `src/components/instruments/*`;
  - `src/components/in-flow/catalog.ts`, `tool-renderer.tsx`, `flow-surface.tsx`;
  - `src/components/editor/extensions/flow-conductor.ts`.

## What to build
An editor loop that reads the draft by itself and finds sentences that need work: grammatical slips, tangled or awkward phrasing, ambiguity, run-ons, dangling modifiers, accidental repetition and the like. For each sentence it finds:
- **Rewrites.** Offer several rewrites (about 3–5) that keep the writer's voice. Label each with what it changes, such as "tighter", "subject up front" or "keeps the rhythm", and show a word-level diff.
- **Apply.** One click applies a rewrite as a single undoable edit.
- **Leave it.** "Leave it" is remembered for that sentence's wording, so the loop doesn't nag.

Decide whether this is a new instrument or editor beside Sentence Bench, or a mode of it, and say why in one or two sentences. Fit the app's existing surfaces and voice; don't add a generic sidebar.

### Running the loop
- **Cost to an idle tab.** A previous release regressed an idle tab to 45% CPU by spell-checking every sentence of an opened document. It was fixed by `seedOpeningWordings` in `sentence-ledger.ts`.
  - Work at idle time and incrementally, on changed sentences only.
  - Cache results by sentence text.
  - Use cheap local signals (Harper findings and simple heuristics) to pick candidates, and spend model calls only on those.
  - Measure idle-tab CPU before and after with `/home/diogenes/.t3/worktrees/twyne/perf-harness/idle-tab.mjs`. Run it from your checkout with `PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_VALIDATE_HOST_REQUIREMENTS=1 env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH node …`.
- **Models.** Reuse the existing plumbing through which Sentence Bench and the room get rewrites and judgements (local, hosted or bring-your-own). Don't add a new provider path.
- **Voice.** UI copy is plain and writerly with no stock caveats. Motion uses the living-press tokens in `src/styles/motion.css` and respects `html[data-motion]` full, calm and still.
- **The manual.** If instruments are listed in the manual (`src/routes/docs/guide-writing-instruments.ts`), add a short entry in its voice.

## Tests and verification
- Unit tests for candidate selection, caching, "leave it" memory, and rewrite parsing and validation.
- Use a browser check with a mocked model: a local OpenAI-compatible stub set as the writer's own provider, or the existing test seams. Check that:
  - flagged sentences appear;
  - rewrites show;
  - applying one changes the text with one undo step;
  - "leave it" sticks across a reload.
- Run only targeted `bun test`, eslint on the files you touched, and one `bun run build` at the end. Don't run the full suite.

## Limits
- Commit on your branch locally.
- Do not push, deploy or open PRs.
- Do not sign in or create accounts against production, and do not trigger paid or hosted AI.
- Do not change Railway variables or Convex env.
- Do not touch `/home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne`.
- Stop your server by the PID on your port. Never use `pkill -f`.

## Report back
- Branch and head SHA.
- The design decision and why.
- What changed, as file:line.
- Idle CPU before and after.
- How you verified, with commands and results.
- Anything open.

input.title: Scene Bench: look, sound and motion via Clairic + fal
input.task:
You are working on Twyne, a local-first writing app (Qwik 2 + TipTap/ProseMirror + Convex). Your goal is to make Scene Bench generate the look, sound and motion of a scene. Here is the request in the user's own words:

> "scene bench we should be getting the entire idea here that scene bench is supposed to give these other multimodal options for modals and what they are making where we get options for what this scene would sound like what it would look the motion everything like that and we get generation there that is created from this. clairic can feed into runs like this for scene bench and then we can use our fal key to create a great visual audio look for what your scenes look like."

## First steps
- Your worktree starts from an older local commit. Begin with `git fetch origin && git switch -c feat/scene-bench-media origin/main`. `main` is v0.27.1. Run `bun install` if the lockfile changed.
- Read `CLAUDE.md`, then `convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md`. Read it before writing any Convex code.
- Read these notes in `/home/diogenes/.claude/projects/-home-diogenes-Projects-apps-twyne/memory/`:
  - `autonomy-by-default.md`
  - `no-reflexive-hedging.md`
  - `skip-long-verification.md`
  - `twyne-browser-verification.md`
  - `notorganic-eval-account.md`
- Run the dev server on **port 5184**: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5184 bun run dev.frontend`.

## What exists today
**Scene Bench**
- Files:
  - `src/components/instruments/scene-bench.tsx` and `.css`;
  - `src/utils/scene-bench.ts`: the scene inventory and dimensions, `createSceneMediaBrief`, `SceneMedium = "image" | "sound" | "motion"`;
  - `src/utils/scene-media.ts` and `scene-media-credit.ts`;
  - `src/components/settings/scene-media-settings.tsx`;
  - `convex/sceneMedia.ts`.
- **Pictures** already generate in two ways:
  - hosted, through the Not Organic gateway route "image", gated by wallet credit and rate limits (`sceneMedia:picture`);
  - through the writer's own provider.
- **Sound and motion** produce only a text brief today.

**Clairic** is the Cloudflare extraction model `@cf/cloudflare/clairic`. The gateway already calls it from `convex/extraction.ts`, and the client side is in `src/utils/extraction-client.ts`, `extraction.ts`, `extraction-contract-v1.json` and `extraction-budget.ts`.

## What to build
1. **A Clairic scene sheet.** Run an extraction pass that turns the selected passage into a structured sheet:
   - setting, time and light;
   - palette and textures;
   - characters and blocking;
   - motion beats;
   - sounds and ambience;
   - mood;
   - suggested framing and camera.

   Mark each field as stated (tied to source spans) or inferred, in the spirit of the existing literal/imagined picture modes. Every generation prompt is built from this sheet. When extraction is unavailable, fall back to the existing local cue scan.
2. **Several takes per medium via fal.ai**, with playback and comparison in the bench:
   - **Look:** a few image variants (literal, imagined, a style).
   - **Sound:** an ambience or soundscape and effects, and optionally a music bed.
   - **Motion:** a short clip, image-to-video from a chosen look.

   Use fal's queue API and **current** model IDs from fal's docs. Look them up; don't guess. Prefer fast and cheap models by default.
3. **Two ways to pay.**
   - **Hosted:** a Convex action calls fal with `FAL_KEY` from Convex env, gated by wallet credit and rate limits like `sceneMedia:picture`. Show the cost per take with the existing cost-label pattern.
   - **The writer's own fal key:** an option in scene media settings, stored the way other provider keys are.
4. **Storage.** Keep generated media locally (IndexedDB blobs) keyed by passage, and keep it out of manuscript evidence.
5. **Running by itself.** Follow autonomy by default within the existing consent. Once the writer has switched generation on in Settings, opening the bench on a scene prepares the sheet, and the first takes generate by themselves within budget. Generate stays as an override. Never run when generation is off.
6. **Voice and motion.** UI copy is plain and writerly with no stock caveats. Motion uses the living-press tokens in `src/styles/motion.css` and respects `html[data-motion]`.

## The fal key
No fal key is in skate or env right now.
- Build and test against a mocked fal endpoint.
- If `skate get fal-key` returns a key later (the user may add one), a few live calls are fine: at most about 6 in total, on the cheapest models.
- Never print the key, and never write it to a file in the repo.
- Do not set Convex or Railway env. Report what env needs setting instead.

## Tests and verification
- Unit tests for sheet parsing and validation, prompt building from the sheet, fal request and polling (mocked), credit gating, and IDB storage.
- A browser check with mocks: open the bench on a scene, see the sheet, see takes for each medium, and play them.
- Run only targeted `bun test`, eslint on the files you touched, and one `bun run build` at the end. Don't run the full suite.

## Limits
- Commit on your branch locally.
- Do not push, deploy or open PRs.
- Do not sign in or create accounts against production.
- Do not change Railway variables or Convex env.
- Do not touch `/home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne`.
- Stop your server by the PID on your port. Never use `pkill -f`.

## Report back
- Branch and head SHA.
- The fal model IDs you chose, with links to the docs.
- What changed, as file:line.
- The env and config needed to ship.
- How you verified, with commands and results.
- Live-call results if a key was available.
- Anything open.

input.title: Flicker and warnings while a model runs
input.task:
You are working on Twyne, a local-first writing app (Qwik 2 + TipTap/ProseMirror + Convex). Your goal is to find and fix a bug the user reported in their own words:

> "there is this scrolling bug where we see a ton of flickering as well when model is going on and just get a lot warnings that something is wrong"

## First steps
- Your worktree starts from an older local commit. Begin with `git fetch origin && git switch -c fix/flicker-during-model-runs origin/main`. `main` is v0.27.1. Run `bun install` if the lockfile changed.

- Read these notes in `/home/diogenes/.claude/projects/-home-diogenes-Projects-apps-twyne/memory/`:
  - `twyne-browser-verification.md`: the headless Playwright recipe and IndexedDB seeding.
  - `skip-long-verification.md`
  - `dev-machine-is-old.md`
  - `no-reflexive-hedging.md`
- Run the dev server on **port 5181**: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5181 bun run dev.frontend`. Other lanes are using 5182–5185.
- Earlier perf harness scripts are in `/home/diogenes/.t3/worktrees/twyne/perf-harness/` (`idle-tab.mjs`, `multi-tab.mjs`, `typing-burst.mjs`, `perf-metric.mjs`). Run them from a Twyne checkout as `PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_VALIDATE_HOST_REQUIREMENTS=1 env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH node <script>`. Reuse or extend them.

## What to investigate
"When model is going on" is ambiguous. Cover every kind of model work the editor runs while the writer scrolls:
- writers'-room and editorial-board runs, and in-flow margin cards arriving or updating (`src/components/in-flow/flow-surface.tsx`, `src/components/editor/extensions/flow-conductor.ts`);
- live review (`src/components/writing-tools/live-review-status.tsx`, `src/utils/live-review.ts`);
- the research loop;
- grammar (Harper wasm, `src/utils/grammar.ts`);
- on-device WebGPU models. Use the Iris Xe Chromium flags from the browser note.

To make model runs happen without production accounts or spend, start a small local mock OpenAI-compatible server that streams slow tokens. Configure it as the writer's own provider (bring-your-own key in Settings, or seed the settings in IndexedDB).

Then scroll the manuscript during those runs, in both Firefox and Chromium. Capture the flicker with evidence, for example:
- layout-shift entries;
- repeated mounts of margin cards (MutationObserver);
- decoration or highlight rebuilds (wet ink uses the CSS Custom Highlight API);
- scroll-anchoring fights (`overflow-anchor`) or programmatic scrollIntoView/scrollTop writes;
- the desk lamp and running foot (`src/styles/motion.css`, `--lamp-x`/`--lamp-y`);
- long frames.

The second half of the report is "a lot warnings that something is wrong". Find exactly which warnings show during runs: UI notices (`ApplicationNotice`, live-review notices, toasts) and console errors. Find why they fire and fix the causes. Where a notice is legitimate, make it show once, not repeatedly.

## Fixes and measurement
- Fix root causes. Don't hide symptoms with blanket `animation: none` or by dropping features.
- Measure the same scenario before and after, for example per 10 s of scrolling during a run:

input.title: Hover cards that stay and can be used
input.task:
You are working on Twyne, a local-first writing app (Qwik 2 + TipTap/ProseMirror + Convex). Your goal is to make the editor's hover cards stay and be usable. Here is the request in the user's own words:

> "the users when they see the hover effect they want to be able to interact with the editor that pops up and we should have a effect where the hover card that appears sticks around while the user has seen it for a time so that the user can go click on it send a reply get the non truncated view."

## First steps
- Your worktree starts from an older local commit. Begin with `git fetch origin && git switch -c feat/hover-cards-stay origin/main`. `main` is v0.27.1. Run `bun install` if the lockfile changed.
- Read `CLAUDE.md`.
- Read these notes in `/home/diogenes/.claude/projects/-home-diogenes-Projects-apps-twyne/memory/`:
  - `twyne-browser-verification.md`: the headless Playwright recipe, IndexedDB seeding, and how to open suggestion cards.
  - `skip-long-verification.md`
  - `autonomy-by-default.md`
  - `no-reflexive-hedging.md`
- Run the dev server on **port 5182**: `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5182 bun run dev.frontend`.

## Where the hover paths are
There are two, and both need the fix.

1. **The floating card when the margin is not carrying notes.** In `src/components/editor/twyne-editor.tsx`, around the comment "Hover: preview a persona note below its sentence" (about line 1980):
   - `mouseover`/`mouseout` on `.twyne-persona-note`, `.twyne-comment-mark` and `.twyne-mark-anchor` drive it;
   - the state lives in `store.notePopover` / `store.userCommentPopover`, with `buildAndPin` and `OPEN_WRITER_COMMENT_EVENT`;
   - there is a 350 ms intent delay;
   - today it closes on mouseout unless `relatedTarget` is already the card. Crossing the gap between the passage and the card closes it.
2. **The margin.** `src/components/in-flow/flow-surface.tsx` uses `hoverId`/`peekId`/`lingerId`/`openId` and `hover()`. Pointing at a passage peeks its card there and draws a connection.

## What to build
A hover card the writer has actually looked at should stay.
- **Dwell.** After the card has been visible for a short dwell (pick it; roughly 600–900 ms), it becomes held. A quick pass-through never holds anything.
- **Crossing the gap.** Add a grace period and treat the pointer heading toward the card (a safe triangle) as staying. Moving from the passage to the card never closes it.
- **While held, the card is fully interactive:**
  - click into it;
  - write and send a reply in its thread;
  - expand it to the untruncated text;
  - use its existing actions.
- **It goes away** on Escape, a click elsewhere, typing in the manuscript, or a deliberate hover on another passage after a grace period.
- **Focus.** It must never steal the caret or focus while the writer is typing. v0.27.1 fixed a focus steal (`src/components/collaboration/share-dialog-focus.test.ts`); don't regress that kind of behaviour.
- **Show the held state.** Use the living-press motion system in `src/styles/motion.css`: tokens like `--dur-settle` and `--ease-set`, and keyframes like `press-impress`. For example, the card settles and pins with a subtle impression. Respect the `html[data-motion]` levels full, calm and still.
- **Zen mode** keeps its current rule: hover previews are suppressed.

## Tests and verification
- Put the hover state machine (intent, dwell, grace, held, dismiss) in a small pure module with unit tests.
- In the browser, use Playwright to:
  - move the mouse from a marked passage to its card across the gap, slowly and with a realistic path;
  - check it stays held;
  - type a reply and send it;
  - expand the full text;
  - check Escape and typing dismiss it, and a quick pass-through does not hold it.
- Check both the floating path (margin hidden) and the margin path.
- Seed a folio with persona notes or comments in IndexedDB. Look at how existing e2e tests seed them (`e2e/`).
- Run only targeted `bun test`, eslint on the files you touched, and one `bun run build` at the end. Don't run the full suite.

input.task:
You are working on Twyne, a local-first writing app (Qwik 2 + TipTap/ProseMirror + Convex). The writer wants an editor that finds the sentences that need work and offers rewrites. Here is the request in the user's own words:

> "we need another editor and loop like sentence bench that looks at sentences that are worded weirdly grammatically or otherwise that need work that give the person a bunch of rewritten options this is kind of what sentence bench was doing."

## First steps
